policies.purpose: To make sure staff are on duty according to the needs of individuals served, that schedules are prepared ahead of time and available for review at the facility, and that DSPs are not pulled from their primary duties.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(D)(4) (checklist item D(4)): [AGENCY NAME] ensures that staff are on duty on the basis of the needs of individuals being served, and that staff schedules are prepared in advance and are available for review at each residential facility. Staffing levels are set from each individual's ISP, assessments, health and behavior support needs, and the time of day, not from a fixed formula. The rule sets no numeric ratio and no awake-overnight requirement; [AGENCY NAME] therefore applies any staffing level, awake-overnight need or supervision level written into an ISP or required by DODD or the county board, and confirms uncertain requirements with them in writing. [AGENCY NAME] provides enough support staff so that DSPs are not pulled from primary duties such as direct support, personal care, medication tasks and community activities (C13).

definitions.definition: Qualified employees actually present and available to provide services at the facility during a given shift.
Employees such as cooks, housekeepers, maintenance workers, drivers and clerical staff who perform non-direct-care tasks so DSPs can focus on direct support.
A DSP's direct support work: assisting individuals with daily living, health, community, behavior support and ISP implementation.

procedures: At admission, at each ISP meeting and whenever an individual's condition or needs change, the Administrator reviews the ISP, assessments, health care plans, behavior support plans and risk plans and writes a staffing needs summary for each shift (including nights), noting any one-to-one, line-of-sight, awake-overnight or transportation needs.
The Administrator confirms with the individual's service and support administrator and the county board when a staffing need is unclear and records the answer.
The Administrator builds a master staffing pattern from those needs for weekdays, weekends, holidays and overnight, and updates it whenever the needs summary changes.

Schedules are prepared in advance for at least [NUMBER OF WEEKS] weeks, signed and dated by the Administrator, and posted or kept in a set location at the facility so that staff and reviewers can inspect them at any time.

The schedule shows each staff member's name, position, and shift start and end times, and identifies the staff member with current first aid/CPR, medication certification or delegated nursing authority needed that shift.

Before posting, the scheduler checks that each person is qualified for the assignment (ST-05, DV-01, DV-02), that new DSPs lacking first aid/CPR are paired with a certified staff member, and that the restrictions in ST-01 are met.
Schedule changes are written on the schedule, initialed and dated by the person approving the change, and communicated to affected staff. The original schedule remains legible.
The staff who actually worked each shift are recorded on a time record or shift log kept separately from the planned schedule, so planned and actual staffing can be compared.
Each shift begins with a handoff in which the outgoing and incoming staff review individuals' needs, health changes, appointments and incident follow-up, and the lead staff member documents it.

Absences are covered in this order: on-call staff, qualified part-time or float staff, then supervisors and the Administrator, with qualification checks. If a shift cannot be covered to meet individuals' needs, the staff member in charge calls the Administrator immediately, and no one is left unsupervised. If safe coverage cannot be arranged, the Administrator arranges alternative supports and notifies the county board and guardians.

The Administrator assigns non-direct-care work (cooking, cleaning, laundry, maintenance, driving, clerical) to support staff as the schedule requires, and checks that DSPs are not routinely pulled from primary duties. A DSP who is repeatedly pulled reports it to the Administrator, who adjusts the schedule or adds staff.
Supervisors review staffing weekly against individuals' needs, incident reports and staff feedback and report any shortfall to the Administrator in writing.
Overtime and break scheduling comply with PS-02.
The Administrator reviews staffing as part of the internal compliance review (IC-01) at least quarterly, comparing schedules to ISP needs and recording corrective actions.
Schedules and time records are retained as required in RC-03 and PS-02 and are produced on request for DODD, county board or other compliance reviews.

responsibilities.duty: Funds staffing sufficient for individuals' needs and support staff positions.
Sets staffing from ISPs and assessments, approves schedules, resolves coverage problems, and reviews staffing quarterly.
Prepare schedules in advance, verify qualifications, post schedules and record changes.
Work their assigned shifts, report absences promptly, and perform assigned duties without leaving individuals unsupported.

documentation: Staffing needs summary by individual and shift
Master staffing pattern
Advance-prepared, dated schedules available at the facility
Schedule-change records
Time records or shift logs showing who actually worked
Shift handoff notes
Coverage and shortfall reports
Quarterly staffing review notes

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (D) Staffing - training plan, personnel records, training records
policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: The operator, Administrator and any staff who create, maintain or review personnel records at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To maintain a complete, accurate and confidential personnel record for each employee, as required by the rule and by the facility's personnel policies.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(D)(6) (checklist item D(6)): [AGENCY NAME] maintains personnel records for each employee in accordance with the residential facility's personnel policies (C14). Each record includes the items required by the pre-hire background investigation rules (C51): the application, documented attempts to obtain references, the results of the database checks, the signed attestation and the signed 14-day charge-notice agreement, and a driving record for any employee who will drive. It also includes training records and certificates, and the other documents listed below. Personnel records are confidential, kept in a locked file or access-controlled electronic system, and released only to the employee, authorized management and regulators. [AGENCY NAME] also keeps the wage and hour records required by the federal Fair Labor Standards Act regulations at 29 CFR 516.

definitions.definition: The file, in paper or electronic form, containing the documents that establish an employee's identity, qualifications, background investigation, training, performance and employment history.
The employee's signed statement, required before hire, about the matters listed in the background investigation rule (see MP-05).

procedures: The Administrator opens a personnel record for each new hire before the first day of work, and records are stored in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system, with access limited to the operator, Administrator and persons the Administrator designates in writing.

The pre-hire section contains: the signed application; documented attempts to obtain references (dates, names, results, including unanswered attempts); the results of the seven database checks (OIG exclusion, abuser registry, nurse aide registry, sex offender registry, SAM, ODM exclusion, and DRC offender search) with date and reviewer initials; the signed attestation; and the signed 14-day charge-notice agreement.

The Administrator places in the record the results of any criminal records check required under MP-05, and a documented decision that the person is eligible. No one is hired who is disqualified under the pre-hire rules (C51).

For any employee who drives individuals or drives on agency business, the record contains the driving record obtained before the employee drives, a copy of a valid license, and proof of insurance as TR-01 requires. The driving record is rechecked at least annually.

The record also contains: proof the employee is at least 18 (or age 16-17 for a direct support assistant, with the required documentation), the ability to read and write English as documented in hiring, job description, position and hire date, and any required certification (first aid/CPR, medication administration, delegated nursing).

The training section holds the certificates and training records required by ST-04, including orientation, rights training, annual training and competency checks, with the description, date, duration and instructor.

The record holds the signed annual abuser registry notice acknowledgments (ST-01), confidentiality agreement (RC-02), health and TB screening documentation as required by HE-02, and acknowledgments of personnel policies and the code of conduct (PS-01).
The record holds performance evaluations, supervisor observations (MP-03), corrective or disciplinary actions, written 14-day charge reports and the operator's decisions, and records of separation.

Wage and hour records, including payroll records and time records, are kept as 29 CFR 516 requires and are maintained in the payroll system with cross-reference from the personnel record (PS-02). Records for tax withholding and other legal employment documents are kept separately from the performance record as the law allows.
Medical information, immigration documents and other sensitive items are kept in a separate confidential section of the record.
Employees may review their own personnel record on written request, at a time set by the Administrator, and may add a statement of disagreement to any disciplinary entry.

The Administrator audits a sample of personnel records at least quarterly (and 100% before each DODD review or renewal) using a checklist of required items and records corrections in the internal compliance log (IC-01).

The Administrator keeps a current roster of all staff showing position, hire date, qualification dates and expiration dates for first aid/CPR, medication certification and any other time-limited item, and tracks it monthly.
Records of former employees are retained as RC-03 provides, and then securely destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion, with the destruction recorded.
Personnel records are produced to DODD, ODM or other authorized reviewers on request and are not otherwise shared outside the agency without the employee's written consent or legal requirement.

responsibilities.duty: Approves personnel policies and ensures records are complete and secure.
Opens and maintains records, audits them, tracks expirations and controls access.
Maintain wage and hour records as 29 CFR 516 requires.
Provide accurate documents, keep certifications current and report changes.

documentation: Personnel record for each employee (application, references, database results, attestation, 14-day agreement, driving record, certifications)
Training records and certificates
Signed acknowledgments
Evaluations and corrective actions
Wage and hour and payroll records (29 CFR 516)
Access log or key control record
Quarterly record audit checklist
Roster of qualifications and expirations

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (D) Staffing - training plan, personnel records, training records
policies.title: Written Training Plan, Competency Methods and Training Records
policies.applies_to: The operator, Administrator, supervisors of direct support professionals, DSPs, direct support assistants, support staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who works with individuals is trained for the work through a written training plan that is tied to individuals' needs and the rule's appendices, shows how competency is established, is updated every 12 months, and is backed by complete training records.
policies.policy: This policy meets: OAC 5123-3-01(C)(5)(b)(v) (item C(5)(b)(v)) — the training plan described in paragraph (D)(7); OAC 5123-3-01(D)(7) (item D(7)) — [AGENCY NAME] develops and implements a written training plan for its administrator, supervisors of direct support professionals, direct support professionals, direct support assistants, support staff and volunteers; D(7)(a) — the plan is consistent with the needs of individuals served, best practice and the requirements in appendices A, B, C and D to the rule; D(7)(b) — the plan describes the method (written test, skills demonstration or documented observation by a supervisor) used to establish competency in each area of training; D(7)(c) — the plan is updated at least once every twelve months and identifies who is responsible for arranging or providing the training and the projected timelines for completion; and D(8) — [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written record of training completed by each of those groups that includes a description of the training completed, the date, the duration and, when applicable, the instructor's name. Specific time limits that apply: DSPs must obtain first aid and CPR training equivalent to the American Red Cross, with an in-person skills assessment, within 60 days of hire, and until then work only with a certified staff member present (C16); supervisors must meet the DSP requirements and complete supervisor training within 90 days of becoming a supervisor (C17); and support staff complete the appendix C training (C17). Direct support assistants (age 16-17) perform only limited duties with a DSP (see DV-01).

definitions.definition: A written document that lists, by position, the required and needed training topics, the competency method for each, who is responsible, and the target completion dates.
The way [AGENCY NAME] confirms a person can do what was taught: written test, skills demonstration, or documented observation by a supervisor.
The training requirements published as appendices to OAC 5123-3-01 for the roles and subjects the rule specifies; the plan crosswalk shows which applies to each role.
Training under the federal occupational safety rule at 29 CFR 1910.1030 for employees with occupational exposure.

procedures: The Administrator, with the operator, writes the training plan using the current text of OAC 5123-3-01 and appendices A, B, C and D, the needs of the individuals served (from ISPs, health care plans and behavior support plans) and best practice. The plan covers the administrator, supervisors of DSPs, DSPs, direct support assistants, support staff and volunteers.

The plan includes a crosswalk table that lists every topic required by the appendices for each position, plus topics from individuals' needs (for example, seizure care, dysphagia and modified diets, communication systems, positive behavior support, mobility and transfers, medication delegation).

The plan states, for each topic, the competency method: written test, skills demonstration, or documented supervisor observation, and the minimum standard (for example, passing score or checklist items). Physical and health tasks always use a skills demonstration or observation.
The plan names who is responsible for arranging or providing each training (title and name) and a projected completion date, such as before working alone, within 60 days, or within 90 days.

The operator approves the plan in writing and the Administrator reviews and updates it at least once every 12 months, and sooner when an individual is admitted, an ISP changes, a rule changes, or an incident shows a training gap. Each update is dated and signed, and the prior version is retained.

New employees complete orientation before working alone with individuals: rights (IC-03), abuse and neglect recognition and reporting (BP-02), incident reporting (BP-03), emergency procedures (FS-01 to FS-04), confidentiality (RC-02), person-centered practice (MP-01), infection prevention including bloodborne pathogens under 29 CFR 1910.1030 (HE-02) and the individuals' specific needs.
No DSP works alone until orientation and individual-specific training are complete and competency is documented.

Each DSP obtains first aid and CPR training, equivalent to American Red Cross courses, with an in-person skills assessment, within 60 days of hire. The Administrator schedules the course in the first week. Until it is complete, the DSP is scheduled only when a staff member who holds current certification is present (ST-02).

Each person who becomes a DSP supervisor must meet the DSP requirements and complete the supervisor training named in the rule within 90 days of becoming a supervisor. The Administrator tracks the 90-day date.

Support staff complete the training in appendix C before performing their duties, and volunteers and direct support assistants complete the training the plan assigns to them before they begin (DV-01, DV-02).

Staff complete refresher and annual training as the plan states, including rights, abuse and neglect prevention, the annual abuser registry notice (ST-01) and bloodborne pathogens at least once a year.
Trainers and instructors are qualified for the topic. Outside instructors (such as Red Cross-equivalent providers) supply certificates, and in-house trainers record their name.

For each training, the trainer or Administrator completes a record containing the description of the training, the date, the duration, the instructor's name when applicable, the staff members who attended and the competency method used and result. Staff sign the record.
Staff who do not demonstrate competency are retrained and re-evaluated before performing the task alone, and the retraining is recorded.

The Administrator keeps a training matrix tracking each employee's required topics, completion and due dates, and reviews it monthly. Overdue items are reported to the operator, and the employee is restricted from related tasks until complete.
Training records are filed in the personnel file (ST-03) and kept as RC-03 requires, and are made available to DODD and other reviewers.
As part of the internal compliance program (IC-01), the Administrator reviews the plan, matrix and records at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the training plan and the annual update, and provides funds and time for training.
Writes and updates the plan, assigns responsibility and dates, tracks completion, keeps records and reports overdue items.
Deliver or observe training, document competency and complete their own supervisor training within 90 days.
Attend and complete training, demonstrate competency, and keep certifications current.

documentation: Written training plan with crosswalk to appendices A-D, competency methods, responsible persons and projected timelines
Annual plan update with operator approval and date
Training records (description, date, duration, instructor name when applicable, attendees)
Competency results (tests, skills checklists, supervisor observation forms)
First aid/CPR certificates and skills assessment proof
Supervisor training completion record
Training matrix
Overdue-training reports

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (D) Staffing - training plan, personnel records, training records
policies.title: DSP, Supervisor and Support Staff Qualifications; First Aid/CPR
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals (DSPs), supervisors and support staff of [AGENCY NAME], including staff in the licensed residential facility at [ADDRESS] and staff who deliver HCBS under the Individual Options waiver.
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who provides direct support, supervises direct support or works in a support role meets the Ohio qualifications, holds current first aid and CPR, and completes required training within the required time frames, so individuals receive safe and competent services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs as a DSP only a person who is at least 18 years of age and who can read and write English (C16). Within 60 days of hire, each DSP must hold first aid and CPR certification from the American Red Cross or an equivalent provider, and the certification must include an in-person skills assessment (C16). Online-only courses do not meet this requirement. Until a DSP holds this certification, the DSP works only when a staff member who holds current first aid and CPR certification is present (C16). Each DSP completes the training in appendix B (C16). Each supervisor must meet every DSP requirement and must complete supervisor training within 90 days of becoming a supervisor (C17). Support staff complete the training in appendix C (C17). Pre-service training for new DSPs includes the DODD training modules, agency orientation, training specific to each individual's ISP, and fire safety. No staff member is assigned to work alone with an individual until the required qualifications and the pre-service items in the written training plan (see ST-04) are complete and documented. Background investigations required before hire are handled under MP-05.

definitions.definition: A person employed by [AGENCY NAME] to provide direct care and support to individuals in the residential facility or under the HCBS waiver.
A staff member who holds current first aid and CPR certification that includes an in-person skills assessment, from the American Red Cross or an equivalent provider.
A staff member designated by [AGENCY NAME] to supervise DSPs or other direct support staff.
Staff who support operations of the facility and who are not DSPs or supervisors (for example, cooks, housekeepers or maintenance staff), who complete appendix C training.

definitions.term: Appendix B, C and D training
definitions.definition: The DODD training content that applies to DSPs (appendix B), support staff (appendix C) and certain volunteers (appendix D).

procedures: Before making an offer, the Administrator or designee confirms the applicant is at least 18 years old by reviewing a government-issued photo ID and records the date of birth in the personnel file (see ST-03).

The hiring manager confirms English reading and writing ability. The applicant completes a short written task during the interview, such as completing a form or writing a brief incident narrative. The reviewer signs and dates the result, and it is filed in the personnel record.
Human Resources confirms the background investigation is complete and the applicant is eligible under MP-05 before any work with individuals.
On the hire date, Human Resources enters the hire date and the first aid/CPR due date (hire date plus 60 days) on the staff training tracker.

If the new DSP does not hold current first aid and CPR with an in-person skills assessment at hire, the scheduler marks the DSP as "not yet certified" on the schedule and assigns the DSP only to shifts on which a certified staff member is physically present (see ST-02).
The Administrator enrolls the DSP in an American Red Cross or equivalent in-person first aid/CPR course with a skills assessment, so the DSP can complete it well before day 60.

The DSP gives a copy of the certification card to Human Resources within 3 business days of course completion. Human Resources verifies that the course included the in-person skills assessment and files the copy.
At 45 days after hire, Human Resources checks the tracker. If the certification is not complete, the Administrator arranges a course date before day 60 and records the plan.

If a DSP reaches day 60 without certification, the Administrator keeps the DSP working only with a certified staff member present and documents the reason and the new course date. The Administrator reviews the cause so it does not recur.

The Administrator or Training Coordinator delivers or assigns pre-service training for each new DSP: DODD modules, agency orientation, ISP-specific training for each individual served, and fire safety training under FS-03. Completion is recorded on the training record (see ST-04).
The Training Coordinator assigns the appendix B training to each DSP and documents completion with dates under ST-04.

When a staff member is promoted or newly assigned as a supervisor, Human Resources verifies that the person meets all DSP requirements and records the supervisor start date and the supervisor training due date (start date plus 90 days).

The supervisor completes supervisor training within 90 days of becoming a supervisor. The Administrator verifies completion and files the record. A supervisor who has not completed the training by day 90 is reported to the Administrator the next business day, and the Administrator documents a corrective plan.
The Training Coordinator assigns appendix C training to each support staff member at hire and documents completion.

Human Resources runs the training tracker monthly and renews first aid/CPR before the expiration date shown on each card. Lapsed certification is treated as "not certified" and the DSP is scheduled only with a certified staff member until renewed.
The Administrator reviews the tracker quarterly as part of internal monitoring (see MP-02, IC-01) and reports gaps to the governing body (see GOV-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all qualifications and training deadlines are met, approves schedules for uncertified DSPs, and verifies supervisor training.
Verifies age, English ability and certifications, maintains the training tracker and personnel records, and alerts the Administrator to approaching deadlines.
Schedules and documents pre-service, appendix B and appendix C training and arranges first aid/CPR courses.
Assigns DSPs who are not yet certified only to shifts on which a certified staff member is present.
Complete required training on time and provide certification copies.

documentation: Proof of age and the English reading/writing check in the personnel file
First aid/CPR certification copies showing the in-person skills assessment and expiration date
Staff training tracker with hire dates, 60-day and 90-day due dates
Pre-service training records, appendix B and appendix C completion records
Supervisor training completion record
Schedules showing a certified staff member present with each uncertified DSP
Corrective-plan notes for missed deadlines

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (E) Administrator and delegation of executive authority
policies.title: Administrator Qualifications, Orientation and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: The Administrator of [AGENCY NAME] and the governing body or operator responsible for appointing and overseeing the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is run by a qualified Administrator who is directly involved in daily operations, completes DODD orientation on time, consents to the required Rapback monitoring, and whose appointment is reported to DODD as required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs an Administrator who is at least 21 years of age (C15). Before appointment, the Administrator provides a birth certificate, Social Security card and government-issued photo ID, and demonstrates written English proficiency. The Administrator must have experience in specialized services and in supervision, program oversight and financial management, and must hold either a bachelor's degree or a high school diploma or equivalent credential with four years of experience, in accordance with the experience and education tiers in OAC 5123-3-01(E) (C15). Within 30 days of appointment, the Administrator completes the DODD web orientation (C15). The Administrator consents to Rapback and completes the background investigation required under MP-05 (C12). The Administrator is directly and actively involved in the day-to-day operation of the facility and is not merely a title holder. If the same person serves as administrator for more than one licensee, [AGENCY NAME] notifies DODD as required (C15). Changes in administrator are reported to DODD within 14 days (C15); see AD-02 for delegation and vacancy.

definitions.definition: The person employed by [AGENCY NAME] who is responsible for the day-to-day operation of the licensed residential facility.
The continuous criminal-records monitoring service in which the Administrator's background check is retained and the agency is notified of new reportable offenses.
The licensee, or the person or entity that holds the license and is responsible for the facility's operation.
The authority to make operating decisions and direct staff on behalf of the operator.

procedures: Before a candidate is offered the Administrator position, the operator reviews a written job description that states the 21+ age minimum, experience tiers, education tiers and day-to-day involvement requirement.
The operator collects a copy of the candidate's birth certificate, Social Security card and government-issued photo ID and files them in the personnel record (see ST-03).
The operator obtains a writing sample or other documented evaluation showing written English proficiency, signs and dates the evaluation, and files it.

The operator verifies the required experience in specialized services and in supervision, program oversight and financial management through résumé review and reference or employer verification, and keeps the verification notes.

The operator verifies the education tier: a bachelor's degree (transcript or diploma copy), or a high school diploma or equivalent credential plus four years of qualifying experience documented by employer verification.

The candidate signs the consent form for Rapback and completes the background investigation under MP-05 before starting. The operator does not allow the candidate to act as Administrator until the investigation is complete and eligibility is documented.
On the appointment date, Human Resources records the date and the orientation due date (appointment date plus 30 days) on the training tracker.

The Administrator completes the DODD web orientation within 30 days of appointment and gives Human Resources the completion certificate, which is filed in the personnel record and the training record.

The operator issues a signed written appointment that lists the Administrator's responsibilities, including day-to-day oversight of staffing, service delivery, records, health and safety, the internal compliance program and communications with DODD.

The Administrator is present at, or directly available to, the facility on a regular schedule and documents oversight activities, such as the monthly schedule review, staff meetings and walk-throughs, in the administrator oversight log.

If the Administrator is also administrator for another licensee, the operator notifies DODD of that fact and keeps a copy of the notice. Before accepting any additional role, the Administrator discloses it to the operator in writing.
When an Administrator is appointed or replaced, the operator notifies DODD within 14 days of the change and keeps a copy of the notice (see AD-02 and GOV-03).
If the operator is a natural person, the operator also consents to Rapback and keeps documentation of the consent.
The operator reviews the Administrator's qualification file annually, confirms it is complete and confirms that orientation, background and Rapback are on file.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies qualifications before appointment, makes the written appointment, notifies DODD of administrator changes and multiple-licensee service, and reviews the Administrator file annually.
Completes orientation within 30 days, consents to Rapback, is directly and actively involved in daily operations, and maintains the oversight log.
Collects and files qualification documents and tracks the orientation deadline.

documentation: Birth certificate, Social Security card, photo ID and written English proficiency evidence
Résumé, experience verification and education verification
Signed written appointment and job description
Background investigation result and Rapback consent
DODD web orientation completion certificate
Administrator oversight log
Copies of DODD notices of administrator change and of multiple-licensee service, if any

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (E) Administrator and delegation of executive authority
policies.title: Delegation of Executive Authority and Administrator Vacancy
policies.applies_to: The operator, the Administrator and any staff member designated to hold executive authority at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure someone qualified always holds executive authority when the Administrator is absent, that medication administration continues to follow the Ohio rules during any delegation, and that an Administrator vacancy is handled with a written plan and timely notice to DODD.
policies.policy: The Administrator designates in writing the staff member who holds executive authority during the Administrator's temporary absence (C15). The delegation names the person, the dates and the scope of authority, and the person delegated is someone who knows the facility's policies and the needs of the individuals. Medication administration remains subject to OAC 5123-3-04(E)(3). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(E)(3) (item E(3)) because [AGENCY NAME] provides that administration of prescribed medication pursuant to sections 5123.42 to 5123.46 of the Revised Code is conducted in accordance with Chapters 5123-6 and 5123:2-6 of the Administrative Code. No delegation of executive authority changes that requirement: only staff who are certified or otherwise authorized under those chapters administer medication, as set out in HC-01 and HC-02. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(E)(4)(a) (item E(4)(a)) because, when the Administrator leaves [AGENCY NAME]'s employ, the operator provides its plan for identifying a new Administrator and identifies the person to whom executive authority is delegated in the interim period (C15). The operator notifies DODD within 14 days of an administrator change (C15).

definitions.definition: The authority to make operating decisions, direct staff and respond to emergencies for the facility.
A planned or unplanned absence of the Administrator, such as vacation, illness or training, after which the Administrator is expected to return.
The time between the end of one Administrator's employment and the start of a qualified replacement.
The staff member designated in writing to hold executive authority during an absence or interim period.

procedures: The operator and Administrator select a primary delegate and a backup delegate who understand the licensing rules, the emergency response plan, and each individual's health and support needs.

The Administrator signs a written delegation that states the delegate's name, position, effective dates (or "during any temporary absence"), and the authority being delegated, and the delegate signs to accept it. A copy is filed in the personnel records and kept at the facility where staff can find it.
The Administrator posts or distributes the delegate's name and [PHONE] to all staff on duty, including the on-call contact, before every planned absence.

For any planned absence, the Administrator briefs the delegate on open incidents, pending reports to DODD or the county board, staffing issues and individuals with changes in condition, and records the briefing date.
During the absence, the delegate carries out day-to-day operations, responds to incidents and emergencies, and contacts the Administrator or operator for decisions outside the delegated scope.

The delegate confirms that medication administration continues only by staff who are certified or authorized under Chapters 5123-6 and 5123:2-6 and that any error is handled under HC-02. The delegate does not authorize any other person to administer medication.
The delegate keeps a short written log of significant decisions, incidents and notifications made during the absence and gives it to the Administrator on return.
If the Administrator leaves employment or can no longer serve, the operator immediately names in writing the person who holds executive authority in the interim and informs all staff the same day.

Within 5 business days of the Administrator's departure, the operator prepares a written vacancy plan that identifies how a new Administrator will be found, who is responsible for recruitment, the target dates and the person holding executive authority in the interim.
The operator checks that any candidate meets the qualifications in AD-01 before appointment and that the background investigation is complete under MP-05.
The operator notifies DODD of the administrator change within 14 days and keeps a copy of the notice and any DODD acknowledgment (see GOV-03).
The operator reviews the vacancy plan weekly until a qualified Administrator is in place and documents the review.
When the new Administrator is appointed, the operator ends the interim delegation in writing and the new Administrator completes orientation within 30 days (see AD-01).
The operator reviews all written delegations at least annually, and whenever the Administrator, delegate or backup changes, and updates the posted contact information.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the vacancy plan, names the interim executive authority, notifies DODD within 14 days and oversees the search for a new Administrator.
Designates delegates in writing, briefs them before planned absences and resumes authority on return.
Exercises executive authority within the delegated scope, keeps the decision log and ensures medication is administered only by authorized staff.
Know who holds executive authority on each shift and follow the delegate's direction.

documentation: Signed written delegation(s) of executive authority and acceptance by the delegate
Posted or distributed delegate contact information
Delegate briefing record and decision log
Written Administrator vacancy plan with interim delegate named
Copy of the notice to DODD of administrator change and date sent
Records showing that medication was administered only by authorized staff during the delegation

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (I)-(J) Direct support assistants and volunteers
policies.title: Direct Support Assistants (Age 16-17)
policies.applies_to: All persons aged 16 or 17 employed by [AGENCY NAME] as direct support assistants, and the DSPs and supervisors who work with them.
policies.purpose: To define the limited role of direct support assistants, to prohibit specific tasks under any circumstances, and to protect young workers and the individuals served.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may employ a person aged 16 or 17 as a direct support assistant. A direct support assistant has limited duties and works only with a DSP, who is present and responsible for the assistant's work (C17). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(I)(4) (item I(4)). A person employed as a direct support assistant will not, under any circumstances: (a) provide intimate personal care; (b) operate a vehicle to transport an individual; (c) administer medication or perform health-related activities; (d) provide any care or perform any task expressly forbidden by the individual; or (e) implement any restrictive measure as defined in rule 5123-2-06. Child-labor requirements for minors, including the hour and task limits in 29 CFR 570, also apply and are followed in scheduling and assigning duties. A direct support assistant is not counted as a DSP in staffing and is not left alone with an individual.

definitions.definition: A person aged 16 or 17 employed by [AGENCY NAME] to perform limited support duties under the direction of a DSP.
Care that involves exposure of private body areas or hands-on help with bathing, toileting, dressing or similar personal hygiene tasks.
Tasks involving health care or health monitoring, such as medication handling, treatments, and delegated nursing tasks.
Any intervention defined as a restrictive measure in OAC 5123-2-06, including restraint and seclusion.

procedures: Before hire, Human Resources confirms the applicant is 16 or 17 using a government-issued ID, collects any age or work certificate required for minors, and files them in the personnel record (see ST-03).
Human Resources completes the background investigation required for employment under MP-05 before the assistant has any contact with individuals.

The Administrator issues a written job description for the direct support assistant that lists the permitted tasks (for example, companionship, recreation, meal-time assistance that does not involve intimate care, housekeeping and community outings with a DSP) and lists the five prohibited tasks (I(4)(a)-(e)). The assistant and a parent or guardian, if the assistant is under 18, sign that they have read it.

The Training Coordinator trains the assistant before first assignment on the job description, the individuals' rights, abuse and neglect reporting under BP-02, fire safety under FS-03, and confidentiality under RC-02. Completion is documented under ST-04.
The scheduler assigns a direct support assistant only to shifts on which a named DSP is on duty and present with the assistant. The schedule shows the pairing.

The scheduler applies the 29 CFR 570 child-labor hour and task limits and any state limits when setting the assistant's hours, including limits on late-night work and hours during school terms, and does not assign prohibited tasks.
The DSP is responsible for directing and watching the assistant. Before each shift, the DSP reviews the assistant's tasks for the day and confirms that each is permitted.
The assistant never provides intimate personal care. A DSP provides all toileting, bathing, dressing and similar assistance, and the assistant leaves the area during these tasks.
The assistant never drives to transport an individual, including in agency or personal vehicles. The assistant may ride as a passenger only when a DSP is also present and driving.

The assistant never gives, hands or handles medication and never performs health-related activities, including delegated nursing tasks, treatments or health monitoring. A DSP or other authorized person performs these tasks under HC-01 and HC-02.
If an individual says that the assistant is not to provide a care task or to perform a service, the assistant does not perform it, and the DSP records the individual's direction in the daily notes.

The assistant is never involved in any physical hold, restraint, seclusion or other restrictive measure under OAC 5123-2-06. If a behavioral emergency arises, the assistant moves to a safe place as directed by the DSP and does not take part in the intervention.
The assistant reports any suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, or incident to the DSP and the Administrator immediately, in line with BP-02 and BP-03.

If a DSP or supervisor learns that a direct support assistant has been given or has performed a prohibited task, the DSP or supervisor stops the task immediately, notifies the Administrator the same day, and the Administrator documents the event, takes corrective action and assesses whether a report is required under BP-03.

The supervisor reviews the assistant's assignments monthly and documents the review. The Administrator reviews the assistant's status at age 18 and, if the person is to continue as a DSP, applies ST-05.

responsibilities.duty: Approves each direct support assistant job description, ensures the five prohibitions and child-labor limits are followed, and corrects any violation.
Verifies age and any required work certificate, completes the background investigation, and keeps records.
Assigns the assistant only with a DSP present and within the child-labor hour limits.
Directs and is present with the assistant and keeps the assistant away from all prohibited tasks.
Performs only permitted tasks and reports concerns immediately.

documentation: Proof of age and any required work or age certificate
Completed background investigation result
Signed job description listing permitted and prohibited tasks
Training records for the assistant
Schedules showing the assisting DSP and hours worked
Monthly supervisor review notes
Incident records for any prohibited task, with corrective action

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-01 (I)-(J) Direct support assistants and volunteers
policies.title: Volunteers
policies.applies_to: All volunteers engaged by [AGENCY NAME], and the paid supervisory staff who supervise them. This policy applies only if the facility uses volunteers.
policies.purpose: To set rules for engaging, screening, training and supervising volunteers so that individuals are protected and volunteers do not perform tasks reserved for trained, paid staff.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(C)(5)(b)(viii) (item C(5)(b)(viii)), the requirement for a written policy on volunteers when the residential facility engages volunteers (C9). [AGENCY NAME] has adopted this policy because it [ENGAGES / DOES NOT ENGAGE] volunteers. If [AGENCY NAME] does not engage volunteers, no person is allowed to provide unpaid services until this policy is activated and the Administrator has approved it in writing. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-01(J)(2)-(5) (item J(2)-(5)): volunteers are under the supervision of paid supervisory staff at all times; volunteers do not provide intimate personal care, administer medication, or perform health-related activities; volunteers who provide more than forty hours of direct service per calendar year complete appendix D training and a background investigation at least once every five years; and [AGENCY NAME] will not engage a volunteer who is on the listed databases or who has a disqualifying conviction within the exclusionary period (C17). Volunteers are not counted in staffing and do not replace paid staff. Background investigations follow MP-05, and the volunteer program is part of the internal compliance program (C10; see IC-01).

definitions.definition: A person who provides unpaid services at or for [AGENCY NAME] without being an employee.
Time a volunteer spends in the presence of, or providing support to, individuals served.
A paid employee who meets the supervisor requirements in ST-05 and is assigned to supervise volunteers.
The DODD training required for volunteers who give more than 40 hours of direct service in a calendar year.
The databases checked during the background investigation under MP-05, and the period during which a disqualifying conviction bars engagement.

procedures: The Administrator decides in writing whether [AGENCY NAME] will use volunteers and records the decision in the governing body minutes (see GOV-01). If no, no volunteers are engaged.
The Administrator assigns a paid supervisor to each volunteer before the volunteer starts, and the volunteer is told that person's name and how to reach the supervisor.
The volunteer completes a volunteer application and signs a volunteer agreement that sets out role, schedule, supervision, confidentiality, and the tasks that are prohibited.

Human Resources runs the background investigation under MP-05 for each volunteer expected to give more than 40 hours of direct service in a calendar year, and for any volunteer the Administrator wants screened for other reasons, and checks the listed databases before engagement.

Human Resources does not engage, or immediately ends the engagement of, any volunteer who is on a listed database or who has a disqualifying conviction within the exclusionary period. The reason is documented without placing detailed background information in the individuals' records.
Human Resources enters each volunteer's start date and the date of the next background investigation (at least every five years) in the volunteer tracking list.

The Training Coordinator gives each volunteer an orientation before the first shift covering individuals' rights, confidentiality under RC-02, abuse and neglect reporting under BP-02, fire safety and emergency response, and the volunteer's role.

A volunteer who gives, or is expected to give, more than 40 hours of direct service in a calendar year completes appendix D training. The supervisor tracks hours monthly, and when a volunteer reaches 30 hours, the Training Coordinator schedules appendix D training so that it is complete by the 40-hour mark.
A paid supervisor is with, or directly supervising, the volunteer at all times that the volunteer is with an individual. The volunteer signs in and out on the volunteer log.

Volunteers never provide intimate personal care (toileting, bathing, dressing, or similar help), never give or handle medication, and never perform health-related activities. The supervisor assigns tasks such as recreation, companionship, and assistance with events and clerical work.
If a volunteer is asked, or an individual requests, to do a prohibited task, the volunteer declines and refers the request to the paid supervisor, who arranges for a DSP to help.
A volunteer reports any suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury or unusual event to the supervisor immediately, and the supervisor follows BP-02 and BP-03.
The supervisor reviews each volunteer's performance at least every six months and notes concerns. The Administrator may end a volunteer's service at any time.

The Administrator reviews the volunteer log and tracking list quarterly as part of the internal compliance program (IC-01), confirms that no volunteer exceeded 40 hours without appendix D training and background investigation, and documents the review.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether volunteers are used, approves each volunteer, and reviews compliance quarterly.
Supervises each volunteer at all times, assigns only permitted tasks and tracks hours.
Runs background investigations, screens against the listed databases, and keeps the tracking list and records.
Provides volunteer orientation and appendix D training.
Follows the agreement, stays under supervision, never performs prohibited tasks and reports concerns.

documentation: Administrator decision on volunteer use
Volunteer applications and signed volunteer agreements
Background investigation results and the 5-year re-check dates
Volunteer tracking list with hours of direct service per calendar year
Volunteer sign-in/out log and supervisor assignments
Orientation and appendix D training records
Quarterly compliance review notes

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-02 (F) Fire safety and emergency response plan
policies.title: Fire Safety and Emergency Response Plan: Approval, Content and Posted Floor Plans
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and individuals at the residential facility at [ADDRESS], and the Administrator and operator responsible for the plan.
policies.purpose: To make sure the facility has an approved written fire safety and emergency response plan, that the plan is shared with the county board, that floor plans are posted where staff can see them, and that exits and fire equipment are kept in working order.
policies.policy: This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1) (item F(1)): [AGENCY NAME] has a fire safety and emergency response plan approved by the state or local authority that, at a minimum, addresses the actions to be taken in the event of a fire, tornado, or other natural disaster (C19). The plan is approved by [APPROVING AUTHORITY NAME] before it is used and again whenever it is revised. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(i) (item F(1)(a)(i)): the plan includes a policy that addresses smoking regulations and the storage of combustible materials. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(ii) (item F(1)(a)(ii)): the plan includes a fire safety training program that includes provisions for rescue, alarm, containment, and evacuation (training delivery and drills are set out in FS-03). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(b) (item F(1)(b)): [AGENCY NAME] shares the fire safety and emergency response plan with the county board of developmental disabilities. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(2) (item F(2)): a current graphic floor plan is posted unobstructed on each floor and in an area most appropriate for the posting of staff information, including (a) primary and secondary means of exit from each floor; (b) location of pull stations and fire control system panels, when applicable; (c) fire escapes; (d) the telephone number of the local fire department or 911; (e) the designated tornado shelter or safe area; and (f) designated meeting places in case of fire. Exits are kept clear and unobstructed, a fire extinguisher is kept on each floor, and, in a facility of five or fewer individuals, a smoke detector is kept on each floor (C19). The plan is consistent with the emergency action plan principles in 29 CFR 1910.38 for staff protection.

definitions.term: Fire safety and emergency response plan
definitions.definition: The written plan describing the actions staff and individuals take in a fire, tornado or other natural disaster.
A drawing of each floor showing the items required by OAC 5123-3-02(F)(2).
The main way out of a floor and an alternate way out in case the main exit is blocked.
A designated outdoor location where staff and individuals gather after evacuating so everyone can be counted.
Materials that can burn or feed a fire, such as paper, cleaning chemicals, paint, gasoline and similar items.

procedures: The Administrator drafts the fire safety and emergency response plan for the facility at [ADDRESS] using the facility layout and the needs of individuals, including mobility, hearing, vision and behavioral needs.
The plan states the actions to be taken for a fire, a tornado, and other natural disasters likely in this area, and who does what on each shift (see FS-02 for weather response and re-entry).

The plan includes the smoking and combustible storage policy. It states where smoking is permitted or prohibited, how smoking materials are discarded, how cleaning supplies, paints, fuels and paper are stored, and who checks storage areas each month.

The plan includes the fire safety training program with provisions for rescue, alarm, containment and evacuation, including who rescues individuals who need help, how the alarm is sounded and the fire department called, how doors are closed to contain the fire, and how everyone is evacuated to the meeting place.

The Administrator submits the plan to [APPROVING AUTHORITY NAME] for approval and records the date submitted, the approval date, and the name of the reviewer. The plan is not treated as final until approval is received in writing.
The Administrator sends a copy of the approved plan to [COUNTY BOARD OF DD NAME] and records the date and method sent. The Administrator re-sends the plan after any revision.

The Administrator prepares a graphic floor plan for each floor showing (a) the primary and secondary exits; (b) pull stations and fire control panels where they exist; (c) fire escapes; (d) the local fire department or 911 number; (e) the designated tornado shelter or safe area; and (f) the meeting places for a fire.

Maintenance posts the current floor plan, unobstructed, on each floor in the staff information area. The Administrator confirms each posting by walk-through within one business day of posting and records it.

The Administrator or designee checks the floor plans at least monthly during the facility inspection to confirm they are posted, visible, current and not blocked by furniture or other items, and replaces them within one business day if they are missing or out of date.
The Administrator updates and re-posts the floor plans, and re-sends the plan to the approving authority and the county board, whenever the layout, exits, shelter area or meeting places change.
Staff check on every shift that exits and exit paths are clear, doors open easily, and nothing blocks the primary or secondary exit. Any blockage is removed immediately and noted in the daily log.

Maintenance confirms that a fire extinguisher is mounted on each floor, is accessible and is serviced as required. It confirms that a working smoke detector is on each floor if the facility serves five or fewer individuals. Staff test smoke detectors monthly, and batteries or units are replaced immediately if a detector fails. Results are recorded on the safety checklist.

The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually and after any fire, tornado or drill that exposes a problem, revises it as needed, obtains approval again for significant changes, and gives staff written notice of changes.
Every new staff member is shown the plan and the posted floor plan during pre-service training before working alone, as required in ST-05 and FS-03. Training is documented in the training record.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and revises the plan, obtains approval, shares it with the county board, posts floor plans and verifies equipment.
Maintains extinguishers and smoke detectors, posts floor plans and keeps exits clear.
Know the plan and floor plan, keep exits clear, test detectors and carry out the plan in an emergency.
Reviews and approves the plan as the state or local authority.

documentation: Approved fire safety and emergency response plan with approval date and approving authority
Smoking and combustible storage policy within the plan
Record of the date the plan was shared with the county board of DD
Graphic floor plans for each floor and the posting verification record
Monthly safety checklist: exits, extinguishers, smoke detectors
Staff training records on the plan
Annual plan review and revision records

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-02 (F) Fire safety and emergency response plan
policies.title: Tornado Shelter, Weather/Disaster Response, Evacuation and Re-Entry
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: operator, administrator, all staff and every individual served
policies.purpose: To make sure every person in the home knows where to shelter during a tornado, what to do during a fire, severe weather or other disaster when staying in the home is safe, what to do and where to go when the home must be evacuated, and how people are allowed back in safely. These procedures are part of the fire safety and emergency response plan required by OAC 5123-3-02(F).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains, as part of its fire safety and emergency response plan, written procedures for tornado shelter, for emergencies that do not require relocation, for emergencies that require relocation, and for re-entry. The plan is approved by the state or local authority and shared with the county board of developmental disabilities, and the floor plans are posted, as required by OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)-(8). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(iii) (designation of a tornado shelter or safe area and the procedure for accessing it); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(iv) (responses to fires, weather-related emergencies or other disasters when relocation is not required); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(v) (responses when relocation is required, including a pre-arranged place to meet in case of physical evacuation); and OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)(a)(vi) (procedure for permitting re-entry following a fire safety drill and/or physical evacuation). Staff protect life first. Property is never a reason to delay shelter or evacuation. Each individual's plan accounts for the person's assessed needs in the ISP, including mobility, hearing, vision, communication and behavior support needs.

definitions.definition: The room or area in the home designated in writing as the safest place to take cover during a tornado warning.
Moving individuals out of the home, by physical evacuation or later transfer to another location, because the home cannot be safely occupied.
The outdoor or nearby location designated in the plan where everyone gathers after evacuating so staff can account for each person.
Permitting individuals and staff to return into the home after a drill or physical evacuation, once the home is determined to be safe.

procedures: Designation of tornado shelter (item F(1)(a)(iii)): The Administrator designates the tornado shelter or safe area, normally the lowest level of the home in an interior space away from windows and exterior doors, and records it as [TORNADO SHELTER LOCATION] in the fire safety and emergency response plan.

The Administrator confirms the shelter can hold all individuals and staff on duty and that the route to it is clear and usable by each person, including wheelchair users and anyone using other mobility equipment. If it is not, a secondary shelter is designated and written in the plan.

The shelter location and the route to it are marked on the floor plans posted in the home, along with exits, extinguisher locations and the pre-arranged meeting place, as required by OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)-(8).

Procedure for accessing the shelter: When a tornado warning is issued, or a tornado is seen, the staff member in charge on duty calls for shelter and directs everyone to the shelter by the posted route. Staff assist each individual according to the ISP and take a head count before and after arrival.

Staff bring the flashlight, battery or crank weather radio, resident roster, emergency contact list, medications and medical supplies, and any communication or mobility devices. These are kept in [EMERGENCY KIT LOCATION]. Everyone stays in the shelter until the warning expires or authorities say it is safe.

Emergencies when relocation is not required (item F(1)(a)(iv)): For a fire that is small, out, and where the building is safe, severe thunderstorm, flooding outside the home, power loss, or similar disaster where the home remains safe, the staff in charge first confirms everyone's safety and takes a head count.

Staff move individuals away from hazards, such as windows during high wind. They keep exits clear. They call 911 for any fire, injury or danger. They use the weather radio or local alerts for updates.

If power is lost, staff use flashlights rather than open flames, keep medication and medical equipment functioning (see HC-04), keep food and drinks safe (see FD-01), and call the Administrator at [PHONE]. Staff document the event and response on an incident or log entry the same shift.

Emergencies when relocation is required (item F(1)(a)(v)): For fire, smoke, gas odor, structural damage, flooding, loss of heat or water, or any other condition that makes the home unsafe, staff immediately move all individuals out by the nearest safe exit and call 911. In a fire, staff activate the alarm and evacuate before trying to control the fire.
Staff assist each individual to evacuate according to assessed needs in the ISP. Staff do not use elevators. Staff close doors behind them if they can do so safely and do not re-enter the home.

The pre-arranged meeting place is [PRE-ARRANGED MEETING PLACE] (outdoors, a safe distance from the home), and an alternate is [ALTERNATE MEETING PLACE]. Both are shown on the posted floor plans. At the meeting place, staff take a head count against the roster and tell the fire department immediately if anyone is missing.

If individuals cannot return, the staff in charge contacts the Administrator at [PHONE]. The Administrator arranges temporary shelter at [RELOCATION SITE], with transportation, medications, records, adaptive equipment and staffing. The Administrator completes the notifications and reports required by FS-04.

Re-entry (item F(1)(a)(vi)): After a fire safety drill, staff in charge announces the end of the drill and individuals return only when all signals are cleared and the staff in charge confirms the home is safe.

After a physical evacuation due to an actual emergency, no one re-enters until the fire department or other authority says the home is safe. The Administrator or staff in charge then checks the home before permitting entry. The check includes safe air, working utilities and alarms, clear exits and no structural hazard.

Staff re-enter with individuals in a calm, orderly manner according to ISP needs, take a final head count, reset or restore fire alarms and extinguishers, and document the time and who authorized re-entry. If the home is not cleared, relocation continues under step 12.
The Administrator reviews each actual emergency and drill within 7 days, updates the plan if needed, and sends revisions to the approving authority and the county board as required.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually, and when the home layout changes, and makes sure all staff and individuals are trained on it (see FS-03).

responsibilities.duty: Provides resources for equipment, alternate shelter and transportation. Ensures the plan is approved and kept current.
Designates the tornado shelter, meeting places and relocation site, posts floor plans, trains staff, reviews emergencies and makes required notifications.
Directs sheltering, evacuation, head counts and re-entry, assists individuals according to the ISP, and documents the event.
Know the shelter, routes and meeting places, and follow this policy.

documentation: Approved fire safety and emergency response plan with shelter, meeting places and relocation site
Posted floor plans showing shelter, exits, extinguishers and meeting places
Emergency event log or incident report with times, head counts and re-entry authorization
Drill and training records (see FS-03)
Plan review and revision notes

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-02 (F) Fire safety and emergency response plan
policies.title: Fire Safety and Tornado Drills and Emergency Training
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: operator, administrator, all staff and every individual served
policies.purpose: To make sure fire and tornado drills are conducted and documented on schedule, and that staff and individuals are trained so they can respond safely in an emergency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] conducts and documents drills and training as required by OAC 5123-3-02(F)(9)-(15). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(9) (at least three fire safety drills in a twelve-month period: one in the morning, one in the afternoon or evening, and one when individuals are routinely asleep); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(10) (at least one tornado drill in a twelve-month period); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(11) (drills may be announced or unannounced and are conducted according to the assessed needs of individuals identified in their individual service plans); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(12) (staff training in fire safety, operation of fire safety equipment and warning systems, and the fire safety and emergency response plan, in accordance with rule 5123-3-01); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(13) (each individual participates in documented training within thirty calendar days of residency and at least once every twelve months thereafter, appropriate to assessed needs); and OAC 5123-3-02(F)(14) (individuals may be trained to assist one another in a fire or other emergency to the extent their abilities permit, without additional personal risk and as indicated in their ISPs; this facility is not an ICF/IID). Drills are practiced as real events. No individual is penalized or put at risk by a drill.

definitions.definition: The rolling or license-year period the agency designates, [DRILL PERIOD START DATE], within which all required drills are completed.
A drill where individuals and staff are told in advance.
A drill where only the person conducting the drill knows the timing.

procedures: Drill schedule: By the first day of each twelve-month period, the Administrator prepares a drill calendar showing at least three fire safety drills (morning, afternoon or evening, and during routine sleeping hours) and at least one tornado drill, so the minimum is not left to the end of the year.

The Administrator sets each fire drill to a different time of day and different shift as far as possible, so that all staff who work in the home take part over the year. At least one drill occurs while individuals are routinely asleep, at [SLEEP-TIME DRILL WINDOW].

Whether a drill is announced or unannounced is decided by the Administrator in light of each individual's ISP and assessed needs. For anyone who may be distressed by an unannounced drill, the ISP team's plan is followed and documented. Both announced and unannounced drills are allowed.

Fire drill conduct: The staff member conducting the drill activates the alarm, and everyone leaves by the nearest safe exit and goes to the pre-arranged meeting place in FS-02. Staff assist individuals as the ISP requires and use the alternate route at least once during the year, as if the primary exit were blocked.
Staff take a head count at the meeting place, time the evacuation, and note delays or problems such as people who needed extra help, blocked exits, or alarms that did not sound.
Re-entry follows the procedure in FS-02 only when the staff in charge announces the end of the drill.

Tornado drill conduct: The staff member conducting the drill announces a mock tornado warning. Everyone proceeds by the posted route to the designated tornado shelter or safe area in FS-02, staff take a head count, and everyone stays for a few minutes before the all-clear is given.

Drill documentation: Each drill is recorded the same day on the Drill Record with the date, time, shift, type (fire or tornado), announced or unannounced, whether individuals were asleep, number of individuals and staff taking part, evacuation or sheltering time, problems found, and the name and signature of the person conducting the drill.

The Administrator reviews each Drill Record within 7 days. If problems are found, the Administrator corrects them, such as clearing an exit, repairing an alarm or retraining, and records the correction. A drill with serious problems is repeated.

Staff training: Each new staff member is trained before working alone on fire safety, operation of fire extinguishers, fire alarm and warning systems, and the fire safety and emergency response plan, including the shelter, routes and meeting places, in accordance with rule 5123-3-01 and the written training plan (see ST-04). Training is repeated at least annually and when the plan changes.
Staff training is documented in the personnel or training record with the date, topic, trainer and method used to confirm competency (see ST-03, ST-04).

Individual training: Within 30 calendar days of an individual's admission, and at least once in every 12-month period afterward, staff train the individual on the fire safety and emergency response plan. The training covers hearing the alarm, exit routes, the meeting place, the tornado shelter and what to do in an emergency, and is given in a way each person can understand, according to assessed needs and the ISP.

Individual training is documented in the individual's record with the date, who conducted it, what was covered and how the person responded. Individuals who cannot participate in some part of the training have the reason and the alternative approach documented.

Individuals helping one another: Where the person's abilities permit, the ISP team may identify individuals to assist others in a fire or emergency, for example by alerting staff. This happens only without additional personal risk to the helper and only when stated in the ISPs. No individual is ever expected to take the place of staff responsibility.
Drill records, training records and any corrective action are kept in [DRILL RECORD LOCATION] and are available to the DODD licensing reviewer on request.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and checks drill completion at least quarterly against the calendar.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the program has time and resources for drills and training.
Schedules drills, assigns who conducts them, reviews records, arranges staff and individual training and corrects problems.
Conducts drills as scheduled, assists individuals, takes head counts and completes the Drill Record.
Take part in drills and training, and know the plan and equipment.
Take part in drills and training to the extent of their abilities and with the support in their ISPs.

documentation: Annual drill calendar
Drill Records for fire (morning, afternoon/evening, asleep) and tornado drills
Staff training records on fire safety, equipment, warning systems and the plan
Individual training records (within 30 days of residency and every 12 months)
ISP notes on drill accommodations and any peer-assistance roles
Corrective action notes

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-02 (F) Fire safety and emergency response plan
policies.title: Emergency Reporting and Relocation Notifications
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: operator, administrator and staff in charge
policies.purpose: To make sure fires and emergency relocations are reported on time to DODD and the county department of job and family services, that families and guardians are told quickly, and that DODD is updated weekly until relocated individuals return or permanently relocate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes the reports and notifications required by OAC 5123-3-02(F)(15). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-02(F)(15)(a) (report to DODD within one business day any fire to which a local fire department responded); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(15)(b) (notify each individual's family member or guardian, as applicable, as soon as possible when an emergency requires relocation); OAC 5123-3-02(F)(15)(c) (report to DODD and the county department of job and family services within one business day when an emergency requires relocation); and OAC 5123-3-02(F)(15)(d) (weekly updates to DODD about relocated individuals until they return or permanently relocate). These reports are in addition to any reportable incident or major unusual incident reporting required under BP-03 and GOV-03.

definitions.definition: Any day other than a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday. The deadline is one business day after the event.

definitions.term: Fire to which a local fire department responded
definitions.definition: Any fire, however small, where the local fire department was called to the home and arrived, regardless of damage.
Moving individuals out of the home because of an emergency, including temporary relocation.

procedures: Immediate response comes first: staff make sure everyone is safe, call 911 and follow FS-02. Reports and notifications begin after safety is secured.

Fire with fire department response: The staff in charge notifies the Administrator at [PHONE] as soon as it is safe. The Administrator or designee reports the fire to DODD within one business day of the fire, using [DODD REPORTING METHOD/FORM].

The report includes the home name and address, license number, date and time, cause if known, fire department response, injuries, damage, whether individuals were relocated, and who is the contact person. The Administrator saves a copy of the report and confirmation of transmission.

Family or guardian notification: When an emergency requires relocating individuals, the Administrator or staff designee notifies each individual's family member or guardian, as applicable, as soon as possible. The notice says what happened, that the person is safe, where the person is, and how to reach staff.

If staff cannot reach a family member or guardian, they keep trying at reasonable intervals using the emergency contact list in the individual's record, and document each attempt with time and method. Staff also notify the individual's case manager or service coordinator at the county board [COUNTY BOARD PHONE] and any other person named in the ISP.

Relocation report: The Administrator reports the relocation to DODD and to the [COUNTY] County Department of Job and Family Services within one business day of the relocation, using [DODD REPORTING METHOD/FORM] and [COUNTY JFS CONTACT].

The relocation report states the reason, date and time, names of individuals relocated, where they are staying with address and phone, who is supporting them, plans for medications and health care, and the expected return date or alternative plan.

The Administrator also notifies the county board of developmental disabilities and shares the plan for continued services, so service coordination and any authorized services can continue during relocation.

Weekly updates: For as long as any individual remains relocated, the Administrator sends DODD a written update at least once every seven days, beginning one week after the original relocation report, covering each individual's location, health and services, and the status of repairs or other housing plans.
Weekly updates continue until each individual has returned to the home or permanently relocated. The final update confirms the date each person returned or moved and the new address, if permanent.

If a relocation becomes permanent for an individual, the Administrator follows TT-01 and TT-02 on transfer and notice, records transfer of medications and records, and informs the family or guardian and the county board.
The Administrator keeps a tracking log of each fire or relocation event with the date, report due date, date sent, recipient and confirmation, and the dates of every weekly update.

Before individuals return, the Administrator confirms the home is safe under FS-02, tells the family or guardian, the county board, DODD and the county JFS that individuals have returned, and updates the log.
If the Administrator is unavailable, the delegate named in AD-02 makes the required reports so that no deadline is missed.
After the event, the Administrator reviews the response and revises the emergency plan if needed (see FS-01), and records any lessons learned.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures safety, calls 911, immediately notifies the Administrator, and begins family/guardian contacts if directed.
Makes all DODD and county JFS reports within one business day, notifies families and guardians, sends weekly DODD updates, and keeps the tracking log.
Ensures resources for relocation and that reporting is not missed in the Administrator's absence.
Completes required reports when the Administrator is unavailable.

documentation: Copy of each DODD fire report and confirmation
Copy of each relocation report to DODD and the county JFS with confirmation
Family/guardian notification log with date, time, method and person reached
Weekly update copies and tracking log
Return or permanent relocation notices
Post-event review notes

policies.title: Admission of Residents, Informed Consent and County Board Notification
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: operator, administrator and admissions staff
policies.purpose: To make sure admissions are lawful, voluntary and informed, based on whether the home can meet the person's needs, decided in writing on time, and reported to the county board, without discrimination, and without exceeding the licensed capacity.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits individuals only in accordance with OAC 5123-3-04(C). Admission is voluntary and requires informed consent. The home admits only individuals whose service needs it can meet, taking into account its ability to keep adequate services for all residents. The home gives a written admission decision to the individual and the referring party within 30 calendar days of receiving the application and referral information. After securing informed consent, it notifies the county board in writing within 14 calendar days of admitting a new resident. Under ORC 5123.20, no one may operate a residential facility, or admit a person with a developmental disability to one, without a DODD license, so [AGENCY NAME] admits only while it holds a valid license. Under OAC 5123-3-01(C)(1), the license is valid only for the licensee, the named premises, the number of individuals on it and its term, and the home never admits beyond the licensed capacity.
