This policy meets OAC 5123-3-05(C)(2): [AGENCY NAME] does not unlawfully discriminate because of disability, race, color, religion, national origin or ancestry, sex, or age, and makes reasonable accommodation to a person's physical, mental or behavioral support needs to the extent required by law unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship.

definitions.definition: The individual's (or legal guardian's, as applicable) voluntary agreement to admission after receiving, in an understandable form, the information about the home, services, rights, costs, risks and alternatives.
The person or agency that referred the individual, such as the county board, family, guardian or another provider.
An accommodation that, under applicable law, would impose significant difficulty or expense, determined case by case and documented.

procedures: Receiving applications: The Administrator logs each application and referral with the date received, applicant name, referring party and information received. The 30-calendar-day decision period starts on the date the application and referral information are received.

Confirm licensure: Before any admission, the Administrator confirms that the home is licensed by DODD, that the license is current for the premises, and that an open licensed bed exists. The Administrator never admits a person above the number of individuals on the license. The license is kept at the facility and shown to anyone who asks.

Gather information: The Administrator collects the individual's assessments, current ISP if any, medical and medication information, behavior support needs, communication needs, mobility needs, funding source, and the preferences of the individual, guardian and family.

Meet the individual: The Administrator or designee meets the applicant, in the person's preferred setting if possible, and tours the home with the applicant. The applicant meets staff and housemates when the applicant and current residents agree.

Assess whether needs can be met: The Administrator, with the nurse where health needs exist, reviews whether the home can meet the person's needs for supervision, staffing, health care, medication, behavior support, accessibility and transportation, and whether the home can keep adequate services for all current residents. The review is documented using [ADMISSION REVIEW FORM].

Nondiscrimination (item C(2)): Decisions are based on the person's service needs and the home's ability to meet them, never on disability alone, race, color, religion, national origin or ancestry, sex or age. The Administrator considers reasonable accommodations, such as ramps, communication aids, adjusted routines or added training, before deciding the home cannot meet a need. Any decision that an accommodation would be an undue hardship is made by the Operator, written with reasons, and kept in the file.

Written decision: Within 30 calendar days of receiving the application and referral information, the Administrator sends the individual and the referring party a written decision, either accepting, or declining with the reasons and any alternative known. A copy is kept in the file. If more information is needed, the Administrator requests it promptly so the 30-day deadline is met.

Informed consent: Before admission, the Administrator explains in plain language, and with communication supports as needed, the services, house rules, rights (see IR-01 and IC-03), the grievance process (see IR-03), costs and fees, funds management (see IC-02), grounds and notice for transfer or termination (see TT-01 and TT-02) and the appeal process (see TT-03). Where there is a legal guardian, the guardian's consent is also obtained.

Consent is voluntary. The individual or guardian signs the consent form. If the person or guardian declines, or consent is not given, the person is not admitted. Questions asked and answers given are documented.

Admission agreement: The home provides a written admission agreement stating the services provided, charges and who pays them, and the rights and responsibilities of each party. A signed copy goes to the individual or guardian, and one is kept in the service record (see RC-01).

Admission day: On admission, staff review the ISP or interim plan, medications and orders, allergies, emergency contacts, belongings inventory (see CL-01), and funds handling (see IC-02). The Administrator confirms staff know the ISP before serving the individual (see SS-01). Fire and tornado safety training is scheduled within 30 days of residency (see FS-03).

County board notice: After securing informed consent and admitting the individual, the Administrator notifies the [COUNTY] County Board of Developmental Disabilities in writing within 14 calendar days of admission, using [COUNTY BOARD NOTIFICATION FORM], and keeps a copy and proof of delivery.

Capacity check: The Administrator keeps a current census and reviews it before each admission and each month to verify the home does not exceed the licensed capacity. Any proposed change in capacity follows GOV-02.

Tracking: The Administrator keeps an admission tracking log with application date, 30-day decision due date, date decision sent, consent date, admission date, county board notice due date and date sent.
The Administrator reviews the admission records annually to confirm compliance and reports any problems to the Operator.

responsibilities.duty: Approves admission policy, ensures the license is current and capacity is not exceeded, and decides any undue hardship question in writing.
Receives applications, assesses fit, issues the 30-day written decision, obtains informed consent, notifies the county board within 14 days and maintains the tracking log.
Reviews health needs and medication needs of applicants and advises on whether the home can meet them.
Review the ISP before serving a new resident and support the person's transition.

documentation: Application and referral log
Admission review of whether needs can be met
Written admission decision sent within 30 calendar days
Signed informed consent and admission agreement
County board admission notification with proof of delivery (within 14 calendar days)
Accommodation and undue hardship determinations, if any
Census and licensed capacity check
Admission tracking log

policies.title: Standards of Service Provision and DSP Restrictions
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: operator, administrator, direct support professionals and all staff
policies.purpose: To set the standards for how services are given to each individual and to set the limits on who may serve and in what condition, so individuals receive safe, person-centered, ISP-based services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows OAC 5123-3-04(D). This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(D)(1): the operator, administrator and staff (a) provide services in a person-centered manner; (b) are able to effectively communicate with each individual; (c) are knowledgeable in the individual service plan before providing services; (d) implement services in accordance with the individual service plan; (e) take all reasonable steps to prevent the occurrence or recurrence of major unusual incidents and unusual incidents; and (f) comply with rule 5123-2-06 regarding behavioral support strategies. This policy also meets OAC 5123-3-04(D)(2): the operator ensures that a direct support professional (DSP) does not (a) provide services to the DSP's minor child; (b) provide services to the DSP's spouse; (c) provide services to the minor child of the administrator; (d) provide services to the spouse of the administrator; (e) administer medication or perform health-related activities unless the DSP meets the applicable requirements of Chapters 4723., 5123. and 5126. of the Revised Code; or (f) use or be under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs, illegal chemical substances or controlled substances that may adversely affect the ability to furnish services while providing services.

definitions.definition: Services built around the individual's own goals, preferences, strengths, culture and choices, as stated in the ISP.
A person who provides direct care and support to individuals in the home.
The written plan developed with the individual and the team that lists the person's outcomes, supports and services.
The tasks defined in OAC 5123-6-01 that may be performed only by staff who meet the requirements of the applicable laws.
Major unusual incidents and unusual incidents as defined by OAC 5123-2-06 and the agency's incident policy (see BP-03).

procedures: Person-centered services (D(1)(a)): Staff offer choices in daily routines, meals, activities, privacy and community participation, and follow each person's stated preferences. The Administrator checks that daily schedules reflect individual choice and not staff convenience.

Effective communication (D(1)(b)): Before working alone, each staff member learns how each individual communicates, including speech, signs, devices, pictures and behavior cues, and uses interpreters or aids when needed. The Administrator confirms and records this in the staff orientation checklist.

Know the ISP (D(1)(c)): No staff member serves an individual until the staff member has read the ISP, including the support strategies, health needs and risk plans that apply to the person, and signed the ISP review sheet. The sign-off is filed in the personnel or training record, with the date.

Implement the ISP (D(1)(d)): Staff carry out services according to the ISP and record what was done each shift in the service notes (see RC-01). A staff member who thinks the ISP is not working or not safe tells the Administrator, who brings the issue to the team. Staff do not change the ISP on their own.

Prevent incidents (D(1)(e)): Staff supervise as the ISP and risk plans require, keep the environment safe, follow health and safety protocols, and report hazards immediately. After any MUI or unusual incident, the Administrator reviews the cause and puts a prevention plan in place to prevent recurrence, following BP-03.

Behavioral support strategies (D(1)(f)): Staff use only the behavior support strategies in an approved plan, and follow OAC 5123-2-06 as set out in BP-01. Staff never use restraint, seclusion or other restrictive measures that are not authorized.

Family restriction (D(2)(a)-(b)): A DSP is never assigned to, and never accepts, work providing services to the DSP's own minor child or to the DSP's spouse. At hire, and annually, each DSP discloses in writing whether any family relationship of this kind exists, and the Administrator checks schedules to keep this from happening.

Administrator family restriction (D(2)(c)-(d)): A DSP is never assigned to provide services to the Administrator's minor child or spouse. The Administrator discloses any such relationship to the Operator, who assigns staffing so that the restriction is met.

Medication and health-related activities (D(2)(e)): No DSP administers medication or performs a health-related activity unless the DSP meets the applicable requirements of Chapters 4723., 5123. and 5126. of the Revised Code, such as certification and nurse delegation where required. The Administrator verifies and records each DSP's qualification before assigning any such task (see HC-01 and HC-02). Staff who are not qualified tell the Administrator and do not perform the task.

Impairment (D(2)(f)): No DSP uses, or is under the influence of, alcohol, illegal drugs, illegal chemical substances, or controlled substances that may adversely affect the ability to furnish services while providing services. Staff who take prescribed medication that may affect their work tell the Administrator before the shift so the assignment can be adjusted.

If a supervisor reasonably suspects a DSP is impaired, the supervisor removes the DSP from duty immediately, makes sure individuals are supervised by another qualified staff member, makes sure the DSP gets home safely, documents observed behaviors, and notifies the Administrator the same day. Post-incident drug and alcohol testing, where used, follows [AGENCY DRUG AND ALCOHOL POLICY].
The Administrator reviews each case, decides on discipline up to termination, and determines whether any incident, neglect or abuse report is required under BP-02 and BP-03.
Supervision: Supervisors observe staff practice and review records at least [SUPERVISION FREQUENCY] to confirm these standards are met, following MP-03.
Annual training: Staff are trained on these standards at orientation and at least annually, and the training is documented (see ST-04).
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and when rules change, and keeps staff acknowledgment forms in the personnel file.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure staffing and assignments comply with the family restriction and that qualified staff are available.
Verifies DSP qualifications, assigns tasks, trains and supervises staff, reviews incidents and enforces the impairment rule.
Know the ISP, communicate with individuals, deliver person-centered services, follow behavior support plans, perform only tasks they are qualified for and report to work unimpaired.
Delegates and oversees nursing tasks as allowed (see HC-01).

documentation: Staff ISP review sign-off sheets
Communication orientation checklist
Annual family relationship disclosure forms for DSPs and the Administrator
Task qualification and delegation records
Fitness-for-duty observation notes and incident reports
Supervision notes
Annual training and policy acknowledgment records

policies.title: Self-Administration of Medication and Delegated Nursing Tasks
policies.applies_to: Licensed residential facility: administrator, direct support staff, delegating nurses and individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals who can manage their own medication are supported in doing so, and that any nursing task given to a direct support staff member is delegated properly by a nurse, with clear oversight and records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows OAC 5123-3-04(E) and Chapter 5123-6 of the Administrative Code. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(E)(1): self-administration or assistance with self-administration of prescribed medication is conducted in accordance with rule 5123:2-6-02 of the Administrative Code. This policy also meets OAC 5123-3-04(E)(2): delegation of nursing tasks, excluding the provision of health-related activities, is conducted in accordance with rule 5123-6-06 and Chapter 4723-13 of the Administrative Code. Chapter 5123-6 (OAC 5123-6-01) defines health-related activities (13 listed tasks), delegable nursing tasks, the delegating nurse, employer oversight, and the medication and treatment error types, including administration by uncertified personnel or without required nursing delegation. Staff do not perform any task that requires certification or delegation unless they are qualified under this policy. Medication administration by certified staff and medication error reporting are covered in HC-02.

definitions.definition: An individual taking or applying the person's own prescribed medication, with or without assistance, as allowed by rule 5123:2-6-02.
Help given to an individual who is directing and carrying out their own medication use, within the limits of rule 5123:2-6-02.
The 13 tasks listed in OAC 5123-6-01 that qualified staff may perform; they are not nursing tasks to be delegated under rule 5123-6-06.
A nursing task that a licensed nurse may, under Chapter 4723-13 and rule 5123-6-06, delegate to an unlicensed person after assessment and training.
The registered nurse (or licensed practical nurse where permitted) who assesses the person and the task, trains and checks the staff member, and is accountable for the delegation.
The agency's duty to make sure delegated tasks and health-related activities are done only by qualified staff, with supervision, records and error reporting.

procedures: Self-administration assessment: Before relying on self-administration, the nurse and ISP team assess whether the individual can safely self-administer, as required by rule 5123:2-6-02. The assessment covers knowing what each medication is for, when and how it is taken, and what to do about missed doses or side effects.

The result is written in the individual's record and in the ISP, including the level of support needed. The assessment is reviewed at least annually, after any change in condition and after any medication error.

Assistance with self-administration: Staff help only in ways allowed by rule 5123:2-6-02, for example reminders, opening containers or bringing the medication to the person, and only while the individual directs and carries out their own use. Staff do not take over and administer the medication unless certified and authorized as set out in HC-02.

Secure storage: Each individual's medication is stored safely, with a locked option for the person where appropriate, and in a way that protects other residents. Storage arrangements are in the ISP and are reviewed by the nurse.

Documentation of self-administration: The record shows the medication list, who is assisting, and whether doses were taken as prescribed. Staff note refusals, missed doses, side effects or concerns the same shift, and tell the Administrator and nurse as required in HC-04.

Identify tasks to delegate: When an individual needs a nursing task that is not a health-related activity, the Administrator asks the nurse to determine whether it can be delegated under rule 5123-6-06 and Chapter 4723-13. If it cannot, a licensed nurse performs it.

Check what is a health-related activity: The Administrator uses the list of the 13 health-related activities in OAC 5123-6-01, kept at [HEALTH-RELATED ACTIVITIES LIST LOCATION], to confirm which tasks are health-related activities and which are delegable nursing tasks. Health-related activities are performed only by staff who are qualified under the applicable Revised Code chapters, and delegation under rule 5123-6-06 is not used for them.

Nurse delegation: Only a delegating nurse delegates a task. The nurse assesses the individual and the task, decides in writing whether delegation is appropriate and safe, trains the staff member, checks competence by return demonstration, and gives specific written instructions, including when to call the nurse or 911.

The Administrator does not allow a staff member to perform a delegated task until the delegation is documented for that individual, that task and that staff member. A delegation covers only the person and the task named.

Employer oversight: The Administrator keeps a delegation record for each delegated task showing the delegating nurse's name and license, the staff member, the individual, the task, the date delegated, the dates of nurse supervision, and the date of reassessment.

Oversight check: The Administrator reviews delegations at least [DELEGATION REVIEW FREQUENCY] and after any change in condition, task or staff. Delegation is withdrawn and documented when the nurse finds a staff member not competent, the person's condition changes, or the staff member leaves.

No unqualified performance: Staff must refuse a task they have not been trained, certified or delegated to perform and tell the Administrator at once. Administration of medication by uncertified staff or without required delegation is a medication or treatment error under OAC 5123-6-01 and is handled under HC-02.

Errors and incidents: Any medication or treatment error, or a refusal or reaction involving self-administration, is reported to the Administrator and nurse immediately and handled under HC-02 and BP-03.
Emergencies: If an individual has a medical emergency, staff call 911 first, then notify the nurse and Administrator (see HC-04).
Review: The Administrator reviews this policy annually, and when rules 5123:2-6-02, 5123-6-06 or Chapter 4723-13 change, and trains staff on updates (see ST-04).

responsibilities.duty: Provides employer oversight, verifies staff qualifications, keeps delegation records, schedules reviews and withdraws delegations when needed.
Assesses individuals and tasks, delegates only appropriate tasks, trains and checks staff competence, supervises and reassesses.
Assist with self-administration within the allowed limits, perform only tasks they are qualified or delegated to do, and report concerns and errors immediately.
Takes part in decisions about their own medication to the extent of their abilities.
Decides on and reviews the level of medication support in the ISP.

documentation: Self-administration assessment and annual reviews
ISP medication support section
Medication list and self-administration notes
Nurse delegation record: delegating nurse, staff member, individual, task, dates of training, supervision and reassessment
Staff competency checks
Employer oversight review notes
Medication or treatment error and incident reports (see HC-02, BP-03)
Copy of the list of 13 health-related activities from OAC 5123-6-01

policies.title: Medication Administration by Certified Staff and Error Reporting
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, supervisors, the administrator and any delegating nurse involved in giving or overseeing prescribed medication or treatments at [AGENCY NAME] residential facilities.
policies.purpose: To make sure prescribed medications and treatments are given safely, only by people legally permitted to give them, and that every medication or treatment error is recorded, reported and corrected.
policies.policy:
This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(E)(3) and OAC 5123-3-04(E)(4).

OAC 5123-3-04(E)(3): [AGENCY NAME] conducts administration of prescribed medication under sections 5123.42 to 5123.46 of the Revised Code and in accordance with Chapters 5123-6 and 5123:2-6 of the Administrative Code. Only staff who hold the required certification under Chapter 5123-6 may administer prescribed medication. A task that requires nursing delegation is performed only after a delegating nurse has delegated it, as Chapter 5123-6 requires. Staff who are not certified, and staff who have not received required delegation, never administer medication or perform delegated tasks.

OAC 5123-3-04(E)(4): [AGENCY NAME] complies with the requirements for reporting medication and treatment errors in OAC 5123-6-07 and OAC 5123-17-02. Administration by uncertified personnel, or without required nursing delegation, is a reportable medication or treatment error. Staff report every error to the supervisor immediately, and the agency reports it within the timelines OAC 5123-6-07 sets. If the error also meets a major unusual incident (MUI) category (for example a medical emergency, hospitalization or suspected neglect), the MUI rules in OAC 5123-17-02 apply as well. Medication and treatment records show the prescriber and the date, time and person who administered each dose or treatment.

No staff member is disciplined for reporting an error in good faith. Errors are used to correct systems and retrain staff.

definitions.definition: Any error defined in OAC 5123-6-01, including administration by uncertified personnel or without required nursing delegation, and errors in the drug, dose, time, route, person or documentation.
Staff who hold the certification Chapter 5123-6 requires to administer prescribed medication.
A licensed nurse who delegates nursing tasks to staff as Chapter 5123-6 requires and provides the oversight that Chapter requires.
The tasks listed in OAC 5123-6-01 that certified staff may perform under Chapter 5123-6.
Major unusual incident reportable under OAC 5123-17-02 (Category A, B or C as defined in that rule).

procedures: Before a staff member is assigned any medication administration duty, the administrator or designee verifies that the person holds the required Chapter 5123-6 certification and that it is current. The designee records this in the personnel record (ST-03) and the training record (ST-04).
The scheduler (ST-02) assigns medication passes only to certified staff. Every shift has at least one certified staff member whenever any individual needs medication administered by staff.

Before a task requiring nursing delegation is performed, the delegating nurse delegates it for the specific individual and staff member. The nurse records the delegation, and a copy is kept in the individual's record (RC-01).

Staff give medication only from a current written prescriber order or pharmacy label. If the label, order or medication record does not match, staff do not administer it and call the prescriber, pharmacist or nurse for direction.
Staff administer medication to the correct individual, with the correct drug, dose, route and time. They check the label against the medication record each time.

Immediately after administering, the staff member records the dose on the medication or treatment record with the prescriber, the date, the time and their own name or initials, matched to a signature key.

If a dose is refused, held or missed, the staff member documents it right away and tells the supervisor or on-call nurse the same shift. Staff do not make up missed doses without prescriber or nurse direction.

When a medication or treatment error is discovered, the staff member first protects the individual: they check for symptoms, call the prescriber, pharmacist, poison control or 911 as needed, and secure medical care (see HC-04).

The staff member immediately notifies the supervisor or on-call administrator. If the error involved administration by uncertified staff or without required delegation, the supervisor immediately removes that staff member from medication duties pending review.

The staff member or supervisor completes the written error report before the end of the shift. It states what happened, who was involved, the medication, the harm or risk, the medical response and who was notified.

The administrator or designee reports the error to the entities and within the timelines OAC 5123-6-07 requires. If the error also meets an MUI category (for example a medical emergency or hospitalization), the designee follows BP-03 and OAC 5123-17-02, including county board notice and submission of the incident report by 3 p.m. the next working day.
If the error may be neglect, the designee notifies the county board within 4 hours of discovery and follows BP-02.
The designee notifies the individual's guardian or authorized representative, and the delegating nurse, of the error and the response. The notification is documented.

Within 7 days of any error, the administrator and delegating nurse review the cause, decide on corrective action (retraining, re-observation, process change, or removal from medication duty) and document it.
The administrator reviews all errors quarterly for trends and reports the results to the governing body (GOV-01) and the internal monitoring process (MP-02).
Medication and treatment records and error reports are kept in the individual's record and retained under RC-03.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures only certified staff administer medication, ensures required delegation is in place, ensures all error reports are made on time, and reviews trends.
Delegates nursing tasks as Chapter 5123-6 requires, observes and oversees staff performance, and advises on the response to errors.
Checks certification before scheduling, removes uncertified staff from medication duties, takes first-line error reports and starts the response.
Administer medication accurately, document at the time of administration, and report any error immediately.
Makes the required notices and reports under OAC 5123-6-07 and OAC 5123-17-02.

documentation: Medication and treatment records showing prescriber, date, time and the person who administered
Staff certification and nursing delegation records
Written medication/treatment error reports and corrective action records
MUI incident reports and county board notification records, where applicable
Guardian notification documentation

policies.title: Medication Disposal and Accounting at Termination or Death
policies.applies_to: All staff responsible for storing, accounting for, disposing of or transferring prescribed medication, and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure prescribed medication is disposed of safely and accounted for on a verified, written record, including when services end or an individual dies.
policies.policy:
This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(E)(5), (E)(6) and (E)(7).

OAC 5123-3-04(E)(5), written disposal procedures: [AGENCY NAME] disposes of prescribed medication only under the written procedures below. (a) Every disposal is verified and recorded by two staff members or by an independent external entity. (b) Dangerous drugs are disposed of in accordance with rule 4729-9-06 of the Administrative Code.

OAC 5123-3-04(E)(6), termination of services under OAC 5123-3-05: (a) the operator completes a written accounting of prescribed medication no later than the last day of residency, verified by two staff members; (b) the operator develops a plan for transfer of prescribed medication to the individual or guardian.

OAC 5123-3-04(E)(7), death of an individual: (a) the operator completes a written accounting of prescribed medication immediately and no later than twenty-four hours after the death, verified by two staff members; (b) the operator and staff cooperate with any investigation by a legally authorized entity; (c) disposal follows the (E)(5) procedures, unless an investigation calls for disposal to be delayed.

definitions.definition: Medication ordered for an individual by a licensed prescriber, including prescription drugs and treatments.
A written count and listing of each medication on hand, with name, strength, quantity and condition, signed and dated by two staff.
A party outside the facility staff, such as a pharmacy or take-back program, that verifies and records the disposal.
A drug whose disposal is governed by OAC 4729-9-06.

procedures: Medication is stored in a locked area. A current count of each medication is kept on its individual medication record.

When medication is discontinued, expired, contaminated, or no longer needed, the certified staff member sets it aside in a locked area labeled "for disposal" and does not leave it with active supplies.
Disposal is carried out only with a second staff member present, or through an independent external entity that records the disposal.

For each disposal, both staff (or the external entity) record the individual's name, medication name and strength, quantity, date, method and reason, and both sign. The record is kept in the individual's record.
Staff dispose of dangerous drugs only by a method that meets OAC 4729-9-06. The administrator confirms the method in writing and trains all staff who handle disposal (ST-04).
Medication is never flushed, discarded in regular trash or given to another individual or staff member except as the disposal method permits.
When the administrator is notified that an individual's services will end (TT-02), the administrator assigns a certified staff member and a second staff member to prepare the final accounting.
No later than the last day of residency, two staff count every prescribed medication, complete the written accounting and both sign it.

Before the last day of residency, the administrator develops a written plan for transferring the medication to the individual or guardian. The plan names who receives it, the date, and what is released. The receiving person signs for what they receive.
On learning of an individual's death, the staff member on duty secures all of that individual's medication in the locked area and tells the administrator immediately (HC-05).
Immediately, and no later than 24 hours after the death, two staff members count the medication and complete and sign the written accounting.
The administrator cooperates with law enforcement, the coroner, DODD, the county board and any other legally authorized entity. Staff provide medication records and the accounting on request.

If an investigator or authorized entity indicates the medication is evidence or must be preserved, the administrator delays disposal, keeps the medication locked, and records who gave the instruction and when.
After any investigation hold is lifted, or if no hold applies, two staff or an external entity dispose of the medication under the disposal procedures above and record it.

The administrator reviews the accounting and disposal records within 3 working days and files them in the individual's record. Any discrepancy is investigated and reported as a medication error or incident under HC-02 and BP-03.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns two staff for accounting and disposal, develops transfer plans, directs cooperation with investigators and reviews records.
Secure and count medication, perform and record disposal with a second verifier.
Directly observes the count or disposal and signs the record.
Receives and signs for transferred medication at termination.

documentation: Medication disposal records signed by two staff or the external entity
Written accounting at termination, signed by two staff and dated no later than the last day of residency
Written accounting at death, signed by two staff and dated within 24 hours
Medication transfer plan and receipt signed by the individual or guardian
Notes on any investigation-related delay in disposal

policies.title: Nursing Oversight, Health Monitoring, Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, supervisors, the administrator and the nurse consultant or delegating nurse for [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals' health is monitored, changes in condition are acted on quickly, emergency medical care is secured immediately, and the right people are notified.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] monitors each individual's health under the individual service plan (ISP) and current clinical orders. Seizure, choking-risk and other health-monitoring procedures follow each individual's ISP and the orders of the prescriber, nurse, dietitian or therapist, and staff are trained on them before working alone with that individual (ST-04).

Nursing oversight: No Ohio rule was located that prescribes a specific nursing level for a licensed residential facility, so the nurse consultant role is the operator's choice. [AGENCY NAME] designates a licensed nurse, [NURSE NAME], as nurse consultant and delegating nurse. That nurse performs any delegation and oversight that Chapters 5123-6 and 5123-17 require for medication administration and delegated nursing tasks (OAC 5123-3-04(E)).

Emergency care: Staff immediately secure medical care in an emergency. A medical emergency is a Category B major unusual incident (MUI); a hospitalization is Category C. Employees immediately report suspected or actual MUIs to the provider's designee, the county board or the DODD hotline, and the provider immediately secures medical care.

Treatment authorization: The individual's record contains a signed authorization to seek medical treatment, or documentation of attempts to obtain one (OAC 5123-3-04(J)).

Notification: [AGENCY NAME] notifies the guardian and the county board of significant changes in condition.

definitions.definition: A new or worsening symptom, injury, behavior, appetite, mobility, mood, or other sign that differs from the individual's usual baseline.
A condition that threatens life, limb or serious harm and needs immediate care. It is a Category B MUI.
The licensed nurse the operator designates to advise on health care and, as needed, to delegate nursing tasks.
A signed consent from the individual or guardian allowing the facility to obtain medical care.

procedures: At admission (AM-01), the administrator collects the signed authorization to seek medical treatment from the individual or guardian. If it cannot be obtained, staff document each attempt with date, method and result, and keep trying.

The nurse consultant reviews each new individual's health history, orders and diet or therapy needs within 7 days of admission and records the review. The review lists items needing individual health-monitoring procedures, such as seizures, choking risk, diabetes or dysphagia.

The nurse consultant and supervisor write or confirm individual health-monitoring procedures consistent with the ISP and clinical orders. Staff are trained on them and sign that they understand (ST-04). A copy is kept where staff can find it.
The nurse consultant makes a nursing visit or review at least [NURSE VISIT FREQUENCY] and records it, including observations and any follow-up with the prescriber.
Staff watch each person on each shift for a change of condition and record it in the shift notes the same shift.
If staff observe a change of condition, they tell the supervisor or on-call nurse immediately. The nurse or supervisor decides whether to call the prescriber, arrange a visit, or call 911.

In an emergency (unresponsive, not breathing, choking not cleared, seizure that does not stop, major bleeding, suspected stroke or heart attack, serious injury), the staff member calls 911 immediately and begins first aid or CPR as trained (ST-05). Staff do not delay for approval.

Staff stay with the individual, send the medication list, the face sheet, the treatment authorization and emergency contact information with the individual, and send a staff member to accompany them if staffing permits.

Staff immediately notify the supervisor or administrator. The designee notifies the county board as OAC 5123-17-02 requires. The medical emergency is a Category B MUI and a hospitalization is Category C, so the designee follows BP-03.

The designee submits the incident report by 3 p.m. the next working day. If the cause is suspected abuse or neglect, the county board is notified within 4 hours of discovery and BP-02 applies; staff alleged in physical or sexual abuse are removed from contact immediately.

The administrator or designee notifies the guardian or authorized representative immediately and informs the county board of significant changes in condition. The notice is recorded with date, time and name of the person reached.

After an ER visit or hospitalization, the supervisor obtains discharge instructions and new orders, the nurse reviews them, and the medication record and ISP-related procedures are updated before the individual's next dose or shift.
Staff follow the individual's seizure and choking-risk procedures exactly as written, and record each seizure or choking event with time, duration, response and outcome.
The administrator and nurse consultant review health-related incidents quarterly for trends and report results to MP-02.
If a staff member believes a person's health need is not being met, they can report to the administrator, the county board or the DODD hotline, and no retaliation is permitted.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the nurse consultant, ensures treatment authorizations are in place, and ensures emergency reporting and notifications are made.
Reviews health needs, advises on health-monitoring procedures, provides delegation and oversight as Chapter 5123-6 requires, and reviews post-hospital orders.
Directs response to changes in condition, ensures staff are trained on individual procedures and starts notifications.
Observe and record health changes, call 911 in an emergency, give first aid, and follow individual health procedures.

documentation: Signed authorization to seek medical treatment, or documented attempts
Nurse consultant reviews and visit notes
Individual health-monitoring procedures and staff training sign-offs
Shift notes recording changes in condition
Incident reports, county board notification and guardian notification records
Hospital and discharge records and updated orders

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, supervisors and the administrator of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure that when an individual dies, the death is reported on time, the right people are notified, medication is accounted for, and investigations are supported.
policies.policy: Every death of an individual is a major unusual incident (MUI). A natural death is a Category B MUI; an unexplained death is a Category A MUI. [AGENCY NAME] notifies the county board within 4 hours of discovery of an unexplained death, and submits the incident report by 3 p.m. the next working day. The designee completes the written accounting of prescribed medication within 24 hours of the death, verified by two staff (see HC-03). [AGENCY NAME] and its staff cooperate with law enforcement and any legally authorized investigation.

definitions.definition: A death expected from a known, documented illness or condition. It is a Category B MUI.
A death with no known cause or in unclear circumstances. It is a Category A MUI.
The time any employee first sees or learns of the death. The 4-hour clock starts then.
The person [AGENCY NAME] names to make MUI reports, [DESIGNEE NAME].

procedures: A staff member who finds an individual unresponsive calls 911 immediately and starts CPR unless there are clear signs of death or a valid do-not-resuscitate order in the record. Staff follow the dispatcher's instructions.
Staff tell the supervisor or administrator immediately. The administrator or designee takes over notifications and decisions.
Staff do not move or clean the area, discard items or alter the scene after a death unless emergency responders need it for care. They keep medication, medication records and relevant items secure.
Staff preserve information about the circumstances: time last seen, condition, who was present, and what happened. Each staff member present writes an incident statement before leaving the shift.

The designee notifies the county board immediately, and in every case within 4 hours of discovery if the death is unexplained, or if there is any suspicion of abuse, neglect, exploitation or other event in that 4-hour category. [COUNTY BOARD MUI PHONE] is posted at the facility.
If abuse or neglect is suspected, staff alleged in physical or sexual abuse are removed from contact with individuals immediately. The designee follows BP-02.

The administrator notifies the guardian or authorized representative and the next of kin as soon as possible. The notice is by phone or in person, not by voicemail or text alone. The date, time and person reached are recorded.
The designee classifies the death as Category A (unexplained) or Category B (natural) and enters the incident report in the required system by 3 p.m. the next working day.

The administrator cooperates with law enforcement, the coroner or medical examiner, the county board, DODD and any other authorized entity, and makes records, staff and the scene available as requested.
Within 24 hours of the death, two staff count all prescribed medication and complete the signed written accounting. Disposal follows HC-03 and is delayed if an investigator requires it.
The administrator informs housemates in a caring, individualized way, offers support and counseling resources, and arranges extra staff presence if needed.
The administrator secures the individual's personal belongings and funds and inventories them with two staff (CL-01, IC-02). Release goes to the legal representative or estate and is documented.
The administrator tells the county board and other service providers (for example, the HPC or day program provider) of the death as needed.
The administrator reviews the death with the nurse consultant within 7 days. Any care concerns are referred to the governing body and MP-02.
The individual's record is closed and retained under RC-03. Records tied to an investigation are not destroyed until the investigation is complete.

responsibilities.duty: Directs response, ensures required notices and the 3 p.m. incident report, notifies family and guardian and cooperates with investigators.
Notifies the county board within the required time and submits the incident report.
Call 911, begin CPR if appropriate, preserve the scene and give written statements.
Count and sign the medication accounting within 24 hours.

documentation: Incident report and MUI classification (Category A or B)
County board notification log with date and time
Staff statements and shift notes
Guardian and family notification record
Medication accounting signed by two staff within 24 hours
Belongings and funds inventory and release record
Investigation correspondence

policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All employees and volunteers who drive or arrange transportation for individuals, and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals have safe, accessible transportation that meets their ISPs, and that every driver and vehicle meets Ohio requirements.
policies.policy:
This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(F)(1)-(5) and OAC 5123-3-04(F)(6).

OAC 5123-3-04(F)(1): [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges transportation in accordance with each resident's individual service plan.
OAC 5123-3-04(F)(2): Each employee who provides transportation holds a valid driver's license.
OAC 5123-3-04(F)(3): Each such employee is covered by valid personal or corporate liability insurance as Ohio law specifies.
OAC 5123-3-04(F)(4): [AGENCY NAME] obtains a BMV driving record for each such employee no earlier than 14 calendar days before initial employment as a driver, and at least once every 3 years afterward. An employee with 6 or more points is prohibited from providing transportation.
OAC 5123-3-04(F)(5): Each such employee must immediately notify the administrator in writing if the employee accumulates 6 or more points or if the license is suspended or revoked. The employee stops driving for [AGENCY NAME] immediately.
OAC 5123-3-04(F)(6): The written policies and procedures on vehicle accessibility, vehicle maintenance and requirements for vehicle drivers are set out in this policy and its procedures.

Vehicles that transport individuals who use wheelchairs or other mobility devices meet the accessibility requirements that apply under federal law, including 49 CFR 37, and are equipped with working lifts or ramps and securement devices.

definitions.definition: The driving record for an employee from the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles, showing license status and points.
Points assessed on a driver's record. Six or more bars an employee from transporting individuals.
A vehicle with lifts, ramps and securement suitable for individuals' mobility devices.
Any employee who transports an individual in a company, personal or other vehicle.

procedures: The administrator identifies each individual's transportation needs from the ISP (mobility device, seating, supervision, medical equipment, seizure or behavior needs) and records them in a transportation plan kept in the individual's record.
Before any employee drives an individual, the administrator or designee verifies a valid driver's license by checking and copying the license, and files it in the personnel record (ST-03).

The designee obtains the employee's BMV driving record no earlier than 14 calendar days before the first day the employee drives and files it. A record with 6 or more points disqualifies the employee from driving.

The designee obtains proof of valid liability insurance (corporate policy or the employee's personal policy as Ohio law specifies) before the employee drives, and re-verifies it at each policy renewal.

The designee obtains a new BMV record for each driver at least every 3 years and tracks due dates on a driver log. A record 14 days before the due date is not required; the record is obtained before the 3-year mark.

Each driver signs a statement acknowledging the duty to notify the administrator immediately and in writing of 6 or more points or a suspended or revoked license. The statement is kept in the personnel record.

On receiving such a notice, the administrator removes the employee from all driving the same day and documents it. The employee may drive again only after the administrator verifies a new BMV record and reinstated license and insurance.

Each company vehicle has a written maintenance schedule (oil, tires, brakes, lights, wipers, lift or ramp) following the manufacturer's recommendations and at least an annual inspection. Maintenance records are kept in a vehicle file.

Before each trip, the driver does a basic safety check (tires, lights, fluid warnings, lift or ramp operation, seat belts, securement straps, first aid kit and emergency contact sheet). Defects are reported to the supervisor, and an unsafe vehicle is not used.

Every occupant uses a seat belt. Wheelchairs and mobility devices are secured with the vehicle's securement system and the occupant uses a lap and shoulder belt. Drivers are trained on lift, ramp and securement operation (ST-04).
Drivers do not use handheld phones while driving, do not drive impaired, and do not leave an individual unattended in a vehicle.
Drivers follow the individual's ISP for supervision and for behavior and medical needs, and carry necessary medications or equipment as the ISP and nurse direct.

If an accident or injury occurs, the driver calls 911 if needed, secures medical care, and notifies the supervisor immediately. The designee treats a significant injury or medical emergency as a Category B MUI and follows BP-03.
The administrator keeps a current list of all drivers with license, insurance and BMV record dates and reviews it at least quarterly. Overdue items remove the driver from driving until corrected.
The administrator reviews these procedures annually under GOV-01.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures only qualified drivers are used, maintains the driver log, and ensures vehicles are maintained and accessible.
Obtains and files licenses, BMV records and proof of insurance on schedule.
Keep license and insurance valid, notify the administrator immediately in writing of 6 or more points or suspension, and operate vehicles safely.
Checks vehicles and equipment, assigns qualified drivers and follows up on defects.

documentation: Driver's license copies and proof of liability insurance
BMV driving records (dated within 14 days before first driving; renewed at least every 3 years)
Driver notification acknowledgement statements and any written notices
Driver log and tracking of due dates
Vehicle maintenance, inspection and lift/ramp records
Individual transportation plans
Accident and incident reports

policies.title: Food, Meals, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, supervisors and the administrator at [AGENCY NAME] residential facilities.
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals receive safe, nutritious meals and snacks they choose and enjoy, including modified or therapeutic diets, and that food is stocked, prepared and stored safely.
policies.policy:
This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(G)(1) through (G)(5).

OAC 5123-3-04(G)(1): [AGENCY NAME] offers daily meals and snacks that meet an individual's nutritional needs and preferences as identified by the individual.
OAC 5123-3-04(G)(2): Modified texture or therapeutic diets are prepared and served in accordance with the written instructions of a physician or licensed dietitian. The instructions are kept in the individual's record under paragraph (J) (see RC-01).
OAC 5123-3-04(G)(3): Meals provide variety, substitutions, and accommodation of individuals' personal preferences and religious beliefs. Individuals participate in meal planning and preparation to the extent of their interest and ability.
OAC 5123-3-04(G)(4): Fresh food sufficient for three days and staple food sufficient for at least five days are available in the residential facility at all times.
OAC 5123-3-04(G)(5): Food is prepared and stored properly and in accordance with health codes to protect against contamination and spoilage. Food is stored separately from potentially harmful non-food items, particularly cleaning and laundry compounds.

definitions.definition: A diet in which food is altered in texture or liquids are thickened, as ordered by a physician or licensed dietitian.
A diet ordered to treat a condition, such as diabetic, low-sodium or renal diets.
Perishable food such as produce, dairy, meat and bread, needed to supply three days of meals.
Shelf-stable food such as canned goods, pasta, rice, cereal and shelf-stable milk, needed to supply at least five days of meals.

procedures: At admission and at each ISP review, staff ask each individual about food preferences, dislikes, cultural and religious practices, allergies and how they like to eat. The answers are recorded in the individual's record.

The supervisor obtains any physician's or licensed dietitian's written diet order (modified texture or therapeutic) and files it in the individual's record. Staff may not alter a diet order without a new written order.

The nurse consultant reviews each diet order and trains staff on preparation and serving, including thickened liquids, textures, portion sizes, positioning and choking-risk procedures (HC-04, ST-04). A diet card is posted in a place staff can see but is kept private from visitors.

Staff and individuals plan menus together at least weekly. The menu offers variety from all food groups, includes the individuals' favorites and cultural or religious foods, and lists substitutes. Menus are posted.
Individuals are offered three meals and snacks daily, and snacks are available between meals. Staff do not withhold food as a consequence or reward.
Individuals who do not want the planned meal are offered a substitute of similar nutritional value. Staff record repeated refusal or weight or appetite change and tell the nurse.
Individuals take part in shopping, planning, cooking, serving and cleanup to the extent of their interest and ability. Staff supervise for safety and do not require participation.
Staff prepare and serve special diets exactly as ordered, and check the diet card each time. They keep others' foods separate from foods an individual has an allergy to.

The supervisor checks stock weekly and confirms enough fresh food for three days and staple food for at least five days for all residents, and records it on a stock checklist. Shortages are corrected the same day.
Staff store perishable food at safe temperatures: refrigerators at or below 41°F and freezers at 0°F. The refrigerator and freezer are checked and logged at least weekly with a thermometer.
Staff wash hands before preparing food, follow safe cooking and cooling practices, label and date leftovers, and discard food that is spoiled or past its date.
Staff store food separately from cleaning and laundry compounds, chemicals and other harmful non-food items, in separate locked or designated areas.
Staff keep kitchen, counters, utensils and storage areas clean, and follow local health code requirements. Pests are reported to the administrator immediately.
The administrator reviews food stock checklists, menus and complaints monthly under MP-02. Individuals' complaints about meals are handled under IR-03.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures food budget, supplies and training, and reviews checklists and diet records.
Reviews diet orders and trains staff on modified and therapeutic diets and choking-risk procedures.
Checks 3-day fresh and 5-day staple stock weekly, posts menus and monitors storage and sanitation.
Offer meals and snacks that reflect preferences, follow diet orders exactly, involve individuals, and store and prepare food safely.

documentation: Individual food preference and allergy records
Physician or licensed dietitian diet orders kept in the individual's record
Posted and archived menus with substitutions
Weekly stock checklist showing 3-day fresh and 5-day staple supplies
Refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Staff training records on special diets

policies.title: Clothing and Personal Belongings
policies.applies_to: All individuals residing in the DODD-licensed residential facility operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all direct support staff, the Administrator and any person who assists with clothing, laundry or personal possessions
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual has adequate, well-fitting, age-appropriate clothing; is supported to choose and care for their own clothing and possessions; has belongings recorded when help is needed to manage them; and never loses belongings through discard or an operator change without proper consent and conveyance.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] ensures that every individual has an adequate amount of personal clothing that is in good repair, well-fitting, and comparable in style to clothing worn by age peers in the community. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(H)(1)-(2) (Item H(1)-(2) — Clothing). The ISP team ensures clothing needs are met for any individual who has no personal funds. Staff encourage each individual to select, purchase and maintain their own clothing and to dress as independently as possible. When an individual has been assessed to need assistance managing personal possessions, [AGENCY NAME] records the individual's clothing and personal belongings within 14 calendar days of admission, updates the record at least annually, adds any single item with a purchase price of $50 or more when acquired, and deletes it when discarded or lost. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(H)(3) (Item H(3) — Inventory of Belongings). [AGENCY NAME] does not discard an individual's clothing or personal belongings without the consent of the individual or guardian. If operation of the facility is transferred, the outgoing operator conveys the individuals' clothing and personal belongings to the incoming operator. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(H)(4)-(5) (Item H(4)-(5) — Discard and Transfer of Operation).

definitions.definition: Items owned by or belonging to the individual, including clothing, shoes, toiletries, electronics, jewelry, furniture, decorations, mementos, assistive devices and similar items.

definitions.term: Assessed need for assistance with possessions
definitions.definition: A need for help managing personal possessions identified through the individual's assessment or ISP process.
People of the same age group in the community who do not have a developmental disability.
The written list of an individual's clothing and personal belongings maintained in the individual's record.

procedures: At or before admission, the Administrator asks the individual and guardian (if any) what clothing and belongings the person is bringing and what the person prefers to wear. Preferences are noted in the record.

Within the admission process, the Administrator reviews the individual's assessment and ISP to determine whether the individual has an assessed need for assistance managing personal possessions. The answer is documented in the individual's record.

If the individual has an assessed need, a designated staff member, with the individual present, completes the Clothing and Personal Belongings Inventory within 14 calendar days of admission. The inventory lists each item, a brief description, condition and the date recorded.

The staff member who completes the inventory signs and dates it. The individual (or guardian, when appropriate) is asked to review and sign. If the person declines or cannot sign, staff document that.

Any single item with a purchase price of $50 or more is added to the inventory on the date it is acquired. The entry shows the item, purchase price, date and how it was obtained. Receipts are filed with the inventory where available.
When an item is discarded or lost, staff delete it from the inventory on the date of discard or loss. They note the date, the reason and, for a discard, who gave consent.

The Administrator or a designee updates the inventory at least annually, no later than the ISP annual review date, and signs and dates the update. The updated version is filed and prior versions are retained (see RC-01).

At least monthly, and at each change of season, staff review with the individual whether clothing is adequate in amount, fits well, is in good repair, and is suitable for the weather and activities. Findings are noted in the record.

Where clothing is worn out, outgrown or missing, staff offer to help the individual shop for replacements. Staff support the person to choose styles, colors and stores comparable to those of age peers in the community.

For an individual without personal funds, the Administrator notifies the ISP team and, as needed, the service and support administrator at the county board, so the team can arrange for the clothing need to be met. The notification and the outcome are documented.

Staff support each individual to do as much of their own dressing, laundry and clothing care as they are able. Teaching and support are carried out as written in the ISP. Staff do not select or restrict clothing in a way that is not part of the ISP or a rights restriction process under IR-02.

Staff may not discard, donate, sell or give away any clothing or belongings without the consent of the individual or guardian. Before an item is discarded, staff ask for consent and document who consented, the date and what was discarded. Items that are unsafe or unsanitary may be set aside and the matter raised with the individual or guardian for a decision.

If an item is reported lost or damaged, staff look for it right away, report the loss to the Administrator on the same day and tell the individual or guardian. If the loss may involve theft or exploitation, the Administrator follows BP-02 and BP-03.

If operation of the facility will be transferred, the Administrator prepares a current inventory, reconciles it with the items on site and, on the transfer date, conveys the individuals' clothing and personal belongings to the incoming operator. The incoming operator signs a receipt listing what was conveyed. A copy of the receipt is kept in each individual's record. See RC-03.

When an individual is transferred or terminated, or dies, the Administrator documents the disposition of clothing and belongings for the written accounting required within 30 calendar days (see RC-01 and TT-02, and HC-05 for a death).
The Administrator spot-checks inventories and clothing adequacy quarterly as part of internal monitoring (MP-02) and corrects any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Determines with the team who has an assessed need for possession management; ensures inventories are completed within 14 days, updated at least annually and kept current; ensures clothing needs of individuals without personal funds are raised with the team; approves any discard only with consent; manages conveyance if operation is transferred.

Supports individuals to choose, buy and care for their clothing; completes and updates inventory entries; records items of $50 or more; reports losses and damage the same day; never discards belongings without documented consent.
Individuals choose their own clothing and decide about their belongings as far as they are able; guardians give or withhold consent when required.
Ensures that clothing needs are met for an individual without personal funds and identifies any assessed need for help managing possessions.

documentation: Clothing and Personal Belongings Inventory (initial, annual updates, and entries for items of $50 or more), signed and dated
Receipts for purchases of $50 or more
Documentation of consent to discard, with date and name of person consenting
Monthly and seasonal clothing adequacy notes
Lost-item reports
Conveyance receipt signed by the incoming operator, if operation is transferred
Disposition of belongings in the 30-day written accounting at termination

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-04 (J) Individuals' service records, confidentiality and retention
policies.title: Individuals' Service Records
policies.applies_to: All individuals residing in the DODD-licensed residential facility operated by [AGENCY NAME]; Administrator, DSPs, nurses and any staff who create, update, store or access service records
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, current and accurate record exists for every individual, that current records are available at the facility, that other required records are accessible and provided to DODD on request, and that a written accounting is completed within 30 calendar days after residency ends.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a record for each individual. The following current records are kept at the residential facility, in accordance with OAC 5123-3-04(J)(1)(a) (Item J(1)(a) — Current Records): (i) a photograph; (ii) legal status; (iii) the individual service plan (ISP), including documentation of informed consent; (iv) a signed authorization to seek medical treatment, or documentation that attempts to obtain one were unsuccessful; and (v) medication and/or treatment records showing the prescriber and the date, time and person who administered each dose or treatment. The following records are kept in an accessible location and provided to the Department of Developmental Disabilities on request, in accordance with OAC 5123-3-04(J)(1)(b) (Item J(1)(b) — Accessible Records): (i) former versions of the J(1)(a) records; (ii) admission and referral records; (iii) all service documentation, including notations of progress; (iv) medical and dental examination and immunization records; (v) records of major unusual incidents and unusual incidents; (vi) major unusual incident investigation files; (vii) reconciliations of the individual's account transaction record under rule 5123-2-07; (viii) records of negotiable items owned by the individual; (ix) records of clothing and personal belongings; and (x) a written accounting completed within 30 calendar days following termination of residency, covering the circumstances of termination, the new address, conveyance of records, identification, prescriptions and medications, disposition of clothing and belongings, and release or disposition of personal funds. Records are kept confidential under RC-02 and retained under RC-03.

definitions.definition: The up-to-date version of each document required to be kept at the facility for the individual.
The individual's legal standing, including whether the person is their own legal decision-maker or has a guardian, and any court orders, as shown by documentation.
Documented agreement by the individual or guardian, after the person has been given information in a way they understand, to the ISP and to services as required.
The summary completed within 30 calendar days after residency ends, covering the items listed in OAC 5123-3-04(J)(1)(b)(x).

procedures: At admission, the Administrator opens a record for the individual and a record-content checklist is placed at the front of the record. The checklist is based on Items J(1)(a) and J(1)(b).

A current photograph of the individual is taken at admission with the individual's agreement (or the guardian's) and kept in the record. The Administrator replaces it at least annually or when the person's appearance changes significantly.

The Administrator obtains and files documentation of legal status (for example, guardianship papers or a statement that the individual is their own decision-maker) before or at admission. Changes in legal status are filed the day they are received.

The Administrator files the current ISP in the record at the facility. The ISP is filed together with documentation of informed consent. If a new ISP or revision is received, the prior version is moved to the accessible file and the new version placed in the current record within 5 business days.

At admission, the Administrator asks the individual or guardian to sign an authorization to seek medical treatment. If the signature cannot be obtained, the Administrator records each attempt (date, method, person contacted and result) in the record. Attempts continue and are recorded until the authorization is signed.

Medication and treatment records are kept at the facility for each individual and show the prescriber, and the date, time and person who administered each medication or treatment. Staff complete the entry at the time of administration (see HC-01 and HC-02). The Administrator reviews these records at least monthly.

The Administrator keeps in an accessible location the former versions of the current records, admission and referral records, all service documentation including notations of progress, and medical, dental and immunization records. Staff file new documentation within 5 business days.
All major unusual incident and unusual incident records, and MUI investigation files, are kept for the individual in an accessible location. See BP-03 for the incident process.
Reconciliations of the individual's account transaction record under rule 5123-2-07, and records of negotiable items owned by the individual, are filed monthly in the record. See IC-02 and IR-04.
The Clothing and Personal Belongings Inventory and its updates are filed with the record (see CL-01).

Staff make service documentation entries on the day of service. Entries are factual, dated, timed where appropriate and signed or initialed with the staff member's full name or an identified initials key. Errors are corrected with one line through the entry, the date and initials; entries are never obliterated.
The Administrator performs a record review at least quarterly using the checklist and corrects missing items within 14 calendar days. Results are reported under MP-02.

Records are available at the facility to authorized staff and are provided to DODD on request. The Administrator copies and delivers the requested records by the date DODD sets and logs what was provided and when.

Within 30 calendar days after an individual's residency ends, the Administrator completes a written accounting. It covers the circumstances of the termination, the new address, conveyance of records, identification, prescriptions and medications, disposition of clothing and belongings, and the release or disposition of personal funds. The Administrator signs and dates it and places it in the record. See HC-03 for medications, TT-02 for notices and HC-05 for a death.

At the time an individual moves, the Administrator provides records and items the receiving provider or guardian is entitled to, obtains a signed receipt where possible, and documents what was conveyed.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the record system; opens and audits each record against Items J(1)(a) and J(1)(b); completes the 30-day written accounting; responds to DODD record requests.
Documents services, medication and treatment, and incidents accurately and on time; keeps records secure at the facility.
Ensures medical, medication and treatment documentation is accurate and complete and is filed in the record.
Provide or sign consents and authorizations; may review the record as allowed by law.

documentation: Record-content checklist for each individual
Photograph, legal status documents, ISP with informed consent, signed medical treatment authorization or attempt log
Medication and treatment records
Former versions of current records; admission and referral records; service documentation with progress notes; medical, dental and immunization records
MUI and UI records and MUI investigation files
Account reconciliations and negotiable-item records
Clothing and belongings records
Written accounting completed within 30 calendar days of termination
Log of records provided to DODD

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-04 (J) Individuals' service records, confidentiality and retention
policies.title: Confidentiality, Privacy and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and students of [AGENCY NAME] who have access to individuals' information, in paper, electronic or oral form
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of information in each individual's record, prevent unauthorized disclosure, honor the individual's right to confidentiality of records, and meet applicable federal privacy requirements.
policies.policy: All information contained in an individual's records is confidential. [AGENCY NAME] maintains records in accordance with state and federal regulations and in a manner that ensures their confidentiality and protects them from unauthorized disclosure, whether the record is on paper or electronic. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(J)(3) (Item J(3) — Confidentiality of Records). Confidentiality of records is also a right of each individual under ORC 5123.62, and staff honor it. [AGENCY NAME] releases information only with a valid authorization from the individual or guardian, or as otherwise permitted or required by law. [AGENCY NAME] designates a privacy officer, trains all staff on confidentiality at orientation, and follows the federal privacy rules that apply to it as a covered entity or business associate: 45 CFR Part 160, 45 CFR 164.502 (uses and disclosures) and 45 CFR 164.530 (administrative requirements).

definitions.definition: Any information in or about an individual's record, including identity, diagnosis, services, medications, behavior, finances, photographs and incident information, in any form.
Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by [AGENCY NAME] in any form, as defined in 45 CFR Part 160.
A signed, dated written permission from the individual or guardian that names who may receive the information, what is released, the purpose and the expiration.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to develop and oversee privacy practices and receive privacy complaints.

procedures: The Governing Body designates a privacy officer, [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], and records the designation in writing. The privacy officer's name and phone number [PHONE] are given to individuals and guardians at admission.

Every new employee, volunteer and contractor completes confidentiality and privacy training before having access to any record and signs a confidentiality statement. The signed statement is filed in the personnel record (ST-03) and training is documented under ST-04.
Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet or locked office at the facility when not in use. Only staff with a job-related need hold keys or access.

Electronic records require individual user names and passwords. Staff do not share log-ins, leave screens unattended or save PHI on personal devices or personal email or text accounts. Devices used for records have screen locks and are kept secure.

Staff discuss individuals' information only with those who need it to provide services, and never in public areas, on social media or with friends, family or neighbors. Visitors are not left alone with records.

Staff release information only with a signed authorization from the individual or guardian, or where law permits or requires release, such as to DODD, the county board, Adult Protective Services, law enforcement, health care providers for treatment, or the Ohio Department of Medicaid. The Administrator or privacy officer reviews any request before release.

Before any release, the staff member verifies the identity of the requester and the scope of the authorization, releases the minimum necessary information when required, and logs the date, recipient, what was released and the staff member who released it.

Individuals and guardians may ask to see or get copies of the individual's record, and staff do not refuse such requests without consulting the Administrator. The Administrator responds promptly and documents the response.
Photographs or videos of individuals are taken and shared only with the individual's or guardian's written permission, and never for non-service purposes without that permission.
Records sent by mail, fax or email are marked confidential, sent only to verified recipients, and sent by a secure method. Email containing PHI uses encryption or a secure portal.

Any suspected unauthorized access, loss or disclosure of information is reported to the privacy officer immediately and no later than the end of the same shift or business day. The privacy officer investigates, documents the facts and decides on notifications and corrective action under applicable law.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to corrective action under PS-01, up to and including termination.
Records no longer needed are destroyed only according to the retention schedule in RC-03, by shredding or secure electronic deletion, and the destruction is logged.

The privacy officer retains documentation required by 45 CFR 164.530 (policies, training records, complaints and dispositions) as stated in RC-03, and reviews this policy at least annually under GOV-01.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees privacy practices; reviews release requests; investigates breaches and complaints; maintains the documentation required by 45 CFR 164.530.
Ensures secure storage and access controls; ensures training and signed statements for all staff; enforces corrective action.
Protect information in every form; share only what is needed and authorized; report suspected breaches immediately.
Designates the privacy officer and reviews this policy annually.

documentation: Privacy officer designation
Signed confidentiality statements
Training records on confidentiality and privacy
Signed authorizations for release
Release log
Breach or unauthorized-disclosure reports and follow-up
Privacy complaints and dispositions
Record destruction log

policies.category: OAC 5123-3-04 (J) Individuals' service records, confidentiality and retention
policies.title: Records Retention and Transfer of Facility Operation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Governing Body and all staff who maintain, archive, transfer or destroy records of [AGENCY NAME]; applies to all individuals' records and agency records created under this manual
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps records for the period required by state and federal rules, destroys them securely only when the period has ended, and conveys individuals' records to an incoming operator if operation of the facility is transferred.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has developed a written records retention schedule for all records in accordance with applicable state and federal requirements. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(J)(4) (Item J(4) — Records Retention Schedule). Before the schedule is finalized, the Administrator confirms the Medicaid record retention period with ODM and DODD and records the confirmation and the periods that apply. HIPAA privacy documentation is retained for 6 years under 45 CFR 164.530(j). Where more than one retention requirement applies to a record, [AGENCY NAME] keeps it for the longest applicable period. If operation of the residential facility is transferred from one operator to another, the outgoing operator conveys to the incoming operator the records specified in OAC 5123-3-04(J)(1), which are the current records and the accessible records listed in RC-01. This policy meets OAC 5123-3-04(J)(2) (Item J(2) — Transfer of Operation).

definitions.definition: A written list of each type of record, the period it must be kept, where it is kept and how it is destroyed.
The licensed operator who is giving up operation of the facility.
The operator who takes over operation of the facility.
The current and accessible individual records described in RC-01 under OAC 5123-3-04(J)(1)(a) and (J)(1)(b).

procedures: Before opening, the Administrator identifies every record type [AGENCY NAME] creates, including individual service records, medication records, incident files, financial and billing records, EVV and Medicaid documentation, personnel and training records, background investigation records, fire and tornado drill records and privacy documentation.
