Reviewer sign-in, requests made and records provided
DODD summary with date-stamp and compliance calendar entry
Plan of correction or appeal and proof of timely submission
DODD responses and any resubmissions
Evidence of correction and follow-up checks
Adverse action notices to individuals and guardians with dates delivered
Governing board minutes

policies.title: Individual Rights, HCBS Settings Requirements, Informed Consent and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All individuals served in the residential facility and by HCBS (Homemaker/Personal Care and Shared Living), and all staff, volunteers and contractors
policies.purpose: To protect the rights of every individual under ORC 5123.62 and the federal HCBS settings requirements, to ensure informed consent and supported decision-making, and to give people accessible communication at no charge.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] safeguards the rights in ORC 5123.62 and meets ORC 5123.63, 5123.64 and 5123.65. Those rights include dignity, privacy, free communication, personal possessions, managing finances according to ability, confidentiality of records, filing grievances without reprisal, freedom from unnecessary restraint, abuse-free living, access to medical care and voting.

Each individual has free access to a telephone, and no signage labels or identifies residents as persons with disabilities (OAC 5123-3-02). The home is accessible, clean, safe and homelike.

The setting supports choice, privacy, dignity and community integration consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4). Any modification of a right or setting requirement is individually justified, tied to a specific assessed need, documented in the person-centered plan and handled under IR-02.

The agency obtains and documents informed consent, supports decision-making, and provides language and communication access, including interpreters and accessible formats, at no charge to the individual, consistent with the ADA (42 USC 12101 et seq.) and Title VI (42 USC 2000d).

definitions.definition: Agreement given by the individual (or guardian when applicable) after the matter has been explained in a way the person understands, including purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives, and the right to refuse or withdraw.
Helping a person understand choices and make their own decisions, using trusted supports and accessible information.
Federal requirements that home and community-based settings are chosen by the individual and support choice, privacy, dignity, community access and control over daily life.
An individually justified limit on a right or setting requirement, documented and reviewed under IR-02.
Interpreters, translated materials, large print, plain language, assistive technology and other means needed to understand and be understood.

procedures: At or before admission (or start of HCBS), the administrator or designee gives each individual and guardian a written statement of rights based on ORC 5123.62. It is explained in plain language and in the person's preferred language or format, and the person signs or otherwise acknowledges receipt. A copy goes in the service record (RC-01).

Rights are posted in an accessible, visible place at the facility in plain language and pictures where helpful. Staff review the rights with each individual at least annually and whenever the individual or guardian asks.

At orientation and annually, all staff, volunteers and contractors are trained on individuals' rights, dignity and privacy, freedom from abuse and unnecessary restraint, and non-retaliation. Training is documented under ST-04.

Before each person is admitted or services begin, the team asks about the person's preferred language, communication method, hearing, vision and literacy needs, and records them in the person-centered plan (MP-01). The needs are reviewed at each plan meeting.

The agency provides qualified interpreters (including sign language), translated documents, large print, plain-language and picture materials, assistive technology and other accessible formats whenever needed, at no charge to the individual or family. Family members and other individuals served are not used as interpreters, except at the person's request in an emergency or when the person asks for it voluntarily.
The administrator keeps a list of interpreter and translation resources with contact information ([PHONE]). Staff know how to get access to them, and the administrator logs each time they are used.

Informed consent is obtained for admission, release of information (RC-02), medical treatment, medication, photographs and media, research, and any rights modification. Staff explain what is proposed, why, risks, benefits and alternatives, and the right to say no, using accessible methods. Consent is documented with the date, the method of explanation and who was present.

Where an individual has a guardian, staff still involve the individual, explain things in a way the person understands and respect the person's preferences. Where there is no guardian, staff presume the person can decide and offer supported decision-making, such as extra time, a trusted advocate, pictures and repeating key points.

Consent can be withdrawn at any time. When the person refuses or withdraws, staff do not penalize them and notify the administrator and the person's team. Refusals of medical care are referred to nursing oversight (HC-04).

Telephone: each individual has free access to a telephone, may make and receive calls privately, and may use their own phone or devices. No fee is charged for use of the facility phone, and staff do not listen to calls unless the person asks for help.

Mail, visitors and privacy: individuals send and receive mail unopened, receive visitors as they choose within a house schedule agreed by the housemates, and have private spaces for personal care, calls and meetings. Staff knock and wait for permission before entering bedrooms and bathrooms.

Voting and community: staff help individuals register, get ballots, get to polling places and learn about candidates if the individual wants. Individuals choose their activities, religion, friends and community involvement, and staff support access to transportation (TR-01).
Personal possessions and finances: individuals keep and use personal possessions (CL-01) and manage their money as far as they are able, with supports as described in IC-02 and IR-04.

No signage, labels or notices identifying individuals as persons with disabilities, patients or clients are posted in common areas, on doors or on belongings. The administrator checks this at each monthly home walk-through (HE-01).

Setting standards: the home follows OAC 5123-3-02 environmental standards and HCBS settings requirements. Individuals choose their roommate where possible, decorate their rooms, set their schedules, choose meals and snacks (FD-01) and have access to the kitchen and common areas, subject only to documented modifications.

Modifications: no right or setting requirement is limited unless the team documents a specific assessed need, the less intrusive methods tried, a plan with a time limit and review, informed consent and the person's agreement, and an assurance that the modification will not cause harm. The administrator follows IR-02 for approval and due process.

Grievances and reprisal: individuals may complain to staff, the administrator, the governing board, their county board or DODD, and may use IR-03. Staff never retaliate. Any suspected reprisal is reported to the administrator at once and handled under BP-02.

The compliance officer reviews rights practices at least quarterly, using observation, interviews with individuals and records review, and includes results in the internal monitoring report (MP-02, IC-01). Findings are corrected within 30 days and reported to the governing board.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures rights are explained, posted and respected, arranges communication access, approves modifications under IR-02 and monitors compliance.
Reviews rights compliance results and promotes a culture that respects individuals.
Respect rights, support choices and privacy, use accessible communication, and report concerns.
Assess communication needs, support decision-making and review any modifications.
Reviews rights practices quarterly and tracks corrections.

documentation: Signed rights acknowledgment for each individual
Posted rights notice and staff rights training records
Communication needs assessment in the person-centered plan
Interpreter and translation resource list and use log
Informed consent forms and notes on how they were explained
Documentation of any modification, consent and review (IR-02)
Monthly walk-through checklist showing no labeling signage
Quarterly rights monitoring reports and corrective actions

policies.title: Rights Restrictions and Due Process
policies.applies_to: All employees, Administrator, clinicians who write behavioral support strategies, and the Human Rights Committee
policies.purpose: To protect the rights listed in ORC 5123.62 (C47) by making sure no right is limited, and no restrictive measure is used, except as a documented last resort with due process, and never for punishment or staff convenience.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses positive measures first. A restrictive measure (chemical, manual or mechanical restraint, a rights restriction, or time-out) is used only as a last resort. Under OAC 5123-2-06(C)(18)-(24) (C39), restraint and time-out are allowed only for risk of harm, and a rights restriction only for risk of harm or legal sanction. No restrictive measure may be used for punishment or staff convenience. Before any restrictive measure is used, the requirements of OAC 5123-2-06(D) (C40) must be met: documentation that positive measures failed, an assessment completed within the previous 12 months, a qualified author, informed consent, Human Rights Committee approval, written guardian notification terms, and review at least every 90 days. This policy also supports the HCBS settings requirement that any modification of a right be supported by an assessed need and documented in the person-centered plan (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F)). No staff member may create or apply a rule, house practice, or informal limit that restricts a right outside this process.

definitions.definition: Any limit on a right under ORC 5123.62, such as access to personal possessions, privacy, communication, money, food, or movement, that is not applied to people generally in the community.
Chemical restraint, manual restraint, mechanical restraint, rights restriction, or time-out, as used in OAC 5123-2-06.
Removal of a person from a reinforcing setting for a short period, as a last-resort measure under the limits of OAC 5123-2-06(C).
The written plan that describes positive measures and, only when needed and approved, any restrictive measure, its justification, and its review schedule.
The committee that reviews and approves restrictive measures before use and at each review.
A person who meets the qualifications in OAC 5123-2-06 to write a behavioral support strategy that includes restrictive measures.

procedures: No employee may impose a restrictive measure on their own authority. The only exception is the narrow emergency use of a measure allowed by the rule, which is reported the same day under BP-03.

When a risk of harm (or legal sanction, for a rights restriction) is identified, the Administrator convenes the person, guardian (if any), county board service and support administrator (SSA), and clinician within 5 business days to review the concern and plan positive measures.
The team writes down every positive measure tried, the dates, who carried it out, and the results. The record must show positives failed before any restriction is considered.

The Administrator confirms an assessment of the behavior and its causes was completed within the past 12 months. If not, the Administrator requests one from a qualified professional before any strategy is drafted.
Only a qualified author writes a strategy that contains a restrictive measure. The Administrator keeps proof of the author's qualifications in the file.

The strategy states the specific risk, the least restrictive measure, when it may and may not be used, who may use it, how use is recorded, how the person is protected from harm, and the criteria for ending it.

The author or Administrator explains the proposed measure to the person in plain language and in the person's communication method. Informed consent is obtained in writing from the person or guardian. If consent is refused, the measure is not used.
The Administrator submits the strategy, the failed-positives record and the assessment to the Human Rights Committee. The measure is not used until the Committee approves in writing.

The strategy records when and how the guardian will be notified of each use and of changes, following the notification terms of the rule. The Administrator makes the notification and documents the date, method and person contacted.
Before using a strategy, each staff member is trained on it and shown to be competent (ST-04). The training roster is filed in the personnel record.

Each time a restrictive measure is used, the staff member records the date, start and stop times, what happened beforehand, the positive measures tried first, the measure used, the person's condition afterward, and staff names, before the end of the shift.
Time-out is limited to 30 minutes per incident and 1 hour in any 24 hours. The room is never key-locked, and the person is under constant visual supervision throughout.
The Administrator reviews all use records weekly. Any use outside the approved strategy is reported under BP-03 and handled as an incident and, if warranted, as possible abuse or neglect under BP-02.

The strategy is reviewed with the clinician, person, guardian and Human Rights Committee at least every 90 days. The review decides whether to continue, change or end the measure, and the result is documented.
The measure ends as soon as the criteria for ending it are met or the Committee withdraws approval, and the person's full rights are restored the same day.
Staff are told at hire and annually that restrictions may not be used as punishment, for convenience, or in retaliation for a grievance. A violation is grounds for discipline (PS-01).
The person and guardian are told they may file a grievance under IR-03 or ask for review of any restriction at any time, without reprisal.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every restrictive measure has the required documentation and approvals, convenes reviews, audits use records weekly, and makes guardian notifications.
Completes or obtains the assessment, writes the strategy, trains staff, and participates in 90-day reviews.
Reviews and approves or declines each restrictive measure before use and at each review.
Use positive measures first, apply only an approved strategy as written, document each use, and report anything outside the strategy.
Receive an explanation, give or withhold informed consent, and take part in reviews.

documentation: Record of positive measures tried and why they failed
Assessment completed within the past 12 months
Behavioral support strategy and author qualifications
Signed informed consent
Human Rights Committee approval and review minutes
Guardian notification log
Use records for each instance, and weekly Administrator audit notes
Staff training and competency records for the strategy
90-day review records

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All employees, Administrator, Governing Body, individuals served, guardians and families
policies.purpose: To give every individual a simple, safe way to raise a complaint, to ensure each complaint is answered and resolved, and to use complaint trends to improve services.
policies.policy: Under ORC 5123.62 (C47), individuals may file grievances without reprisal. [AGENCY NAME] gives each individual and guardian the written grievance procedure at admission, in a form the person understands, and accepts grievances in any form, including spoken, written, sign, assistive technology, or through an advocate. Every grievance, the response and the resolution is recorded, and the Governing Body reviews grievance trends. Information about Disability Rights Ohio appears in every notice of transfer or termination (OAC 5123-3-05(C), C28), and the same contact information is posted and given with this procedure. Retaliation against anyone who files or supports a grievance is prohibited. Grievances that allege abuse, neglect, exploitation or other reportable incidents are handled under BP-02 and BP-03 at once and are not delayed by this process. This policy supports the HCBS requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Any complaint or expression of dissatisfaction by or for an individual about services, staff, rights, the home, or another resident, whether or not the person uses the word 'grievance'.
Any adverse action, threat, change in treatment, or discipline taken because a person filed, supported, or took part in a grievance.
A person chosen by the individual, such as a guardian, family member, friend, SSA, or Disability Rights Ohio staff, who helps the person raise a concern.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator or designee gives the individual and guardian the written grievance procedure and reviews it in plain language, using the person's communication method, large print, translation or interpreter as needed (IR-01). The person or guardian signs that it was explained.

The procedure lists how to complain to the Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE]; the county board at [COUNTY BOARD PHONE]; DODD at 1-800-617-6733 (confirm this number against the DODD website each year); and Disability Rights Ohio at [DISABILITY RIGHTS OHIO PHONE]. It states that the person may go outside the agency at any time.
The same information is posted in a common area at the person's eye level, and is re-explained at each annual plan meeting and whenever the person asks.

Any staff member who receives a grievance accepts it without argument, records the person's words as closely as possible on the grievance form, and gives it to the Administrator by the end of the shift.

If the grievance alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, a health or safety risk, or another reportable incident, the staff member also follows BP-02 and BP-03 immediately. The Administrator confirms that report was made.
The Administrator logs the grievance within 1 business day with date received, who raised it, the nature of the concern, and who is helping the person.
The Administrator acknowledges the grievance to the person (and guardian, if the person agrees) within 1 business day and explains the next steps.
The Administrator investigates and gives a written or otherwise accessible response within 10 calendar days. If more time is needed, the person is told why and given a new date.

The person may ask for a review of the response by the Governing Body chair, the county board SSA or Disability Rights Ohio. The Administrator makes these contacts easy and helps the person reach them if asked.
The Administrator records the response, any corrective action, the date resolved, and whether the person was satisfied. If the person is not satisfied, this is recorded with the options offered.
If the grievance involves a right restriction, the Administrator also refers it for review under IR-02. If it involves transfer or termination, the person is directed to the appeal process in TT-03.

Staff are trained at hire and annually that retaliation is prohibited. Any report of reprisal is investigated by the Administrator or, if the Administrator is involved, the Governing Body chair, and may lead to discipline up to termination (PS-01).
The Administrator checks in with the person within 30 days of resolution to confirm no reprisal or recurrence occurred, and documents the check.

Each quarter, the Administrator summarizes grievances by type, location, staff involved, time to resolve and outcome, without naming people when sharing outside the file, and presents the summary to the Governing Body (GOV-01). The Governing Body records actions taken on trends.
The grievance summary is included in the internal monitoring process under MP-02 and IC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Distributes the procedure, logs and investigates grievances, responds on time, protects against reprisal, and reports trends to the Governing Body.
Accept every complaint respectfully, pass it to the Administrator the same shift, and never retaliate.
Reviews grievance trends at least quarterly, handles grievances involving the Administrator, and directs corrective action.
May raise a concern in any way, at any time, inside or outside the agency, without fear of reprisal.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of the grievance procedure at admission
Grievance log with date, concern, response, resolution and satisfaction
Grievance forms and written or recorded responses
30-day follow-up note
Quarterly trend summary and Governing Body minutes
Posted notice with current contact numbers

policies.title: Personal Funds and Property Management
policies.applies_to: Administrator, fiscal staff, all employees who handle money or belongings, individuals and guardians
policies.purpose: To protect each individual's right to manage money and possessions to the extent of their ability, and to prevent loss, misuse or exploitation of funds and property.
policies.policy: Under ORC 5123.62 (C47), individuals have the right to keep personal possessions and manage their finances according to their ability. [AGENCY NAME] lets each person control their own funds to the extent of their ability, supports them in building skills, and never uses personal funds for agency expenses. Individuals' funds are kept separate from operating funds, with a transaction ledger that is reconciled regularly under DODD's rule on individuals' funds as it applies to the agency. The agency's internal compliance program covers management of individuals' funds (OAC 5123-3-01(C)(5), C10). Belongings, and negotiable items where the person's assessed need calls for it, are inventoried as required by OAC 5123-3-04(G)-(H) (C26), including an inventory within 14 days of admission when assessed need requires it. The 2026 SSI federal benefit rate is $994 per month; any room-and-board charge is confirmed in writing with DODD and the county board before it is collected, and is never collected on assumption. Staff may not borrow from, lend to, accept gifts from, or hold a financial interest in an individual's funds or property (PS-01). This policy is part of the Internal Compliance Program (IC-01, IC-02).

definitions.definition: Money belonging to an individual from any source, including SSI, wages, benefits, gifts and personal allowance, held in the person's own control or by the agency on the person's behalf.
A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to receive and manage a person's benefits (20 CFR 416 governs SSI).
Items that can be readily converted to cash or used as money, such as checks, cash, debit cards, gift cards and similar items.
The agency's own money, which must never be mixed with individuals' funds.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator and the person (and guardian, if any) review the person's income sources, who the representative payee is, and the person's ability to manage money, using the ISP and SSA information. The assessment of ability is written and updated at least annually and when the ISP changes.
The person keeps and controls as much of their own money as their ability allows. Any limit on money control is supported by an assessed need and is handled as a rights restriction under IR-02.

If the agency is asked to hold funds, the person or guardian signs a written authorization stating what is held, how the person may get money, and that the person may withdraw funds at reasonable times. The agency never takes control of funds without this authorization or a court or payee order.

Fiscal staff open a separate account, or a separate tracked sub-account, for each person. Individuals' funds are never deposited into or paid from operating accounts and are never commingled with another person's funds.

Staff post every deposit and withdrawal to the individual's ledger on the day it happens. Each entry shows date, amount, purpose, balance, and staff and person signatures, plus a receipt for every purchase.
Two people (staff and the individual, or two staff when the person cannot sign) count and sign for cash on hand each time funds are handed over or returned.

The Administrator, or someone other than the staff member who keeps the ledger, reconciles each ledger to the bank statement and cash on hand monthly, signs the reconciliation, and resolves differences within 5 business days.

Before any room-and-board charge is collected, the Administrator confirms in writing with DODD and the county board that the amount is allowed. The agreed amount, what it covers and the person's consent are documented. The charge must leave the person with enough income for personal needs, taking the $994 monthly SSI federal benefit rate into account where SSI is the person's income.
The agency does not charge individuals for items or services the facility must provide or for Medicaid-covered services, and does not charge fees that are not in the written agreement.

Within 14 days of admission, when the person's assessed need calls for it, staff and the person complete a written inventory of belongings and any negotiable items. The inventory is signed, dated, and updated when items are added or removed and at least annually.
Personal belongings are stored where the person can reach them. Staff do not search, take or restrict possessions except under an approved process (IR-02).

Staff report any missing money or property to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator opens an incident under BP-03, notifies the guardian and the county board as required, and, if exploitation is suspected, reports under BP-02.
The agency repays any individual's funds that were lost or misused through its own error or by staff, within 30 days of determination, and documents it.

When a person moves out, transfers, or dies, the Administrator provides a final accounting, returns all funds and belongings to the person, guardian, or estate representative, and gets a signed receipt. Death-related handling follows HC-05 and RC-03.
The Administrator reviews a sample of ledgers, receipts and inventories quarterly as part of the internal compliance program and reports exceptions to the Governing Body (IC-01, IC-02, MP-02).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees fund and property systems, confirms any room-and-board charge in writing before collection, and reports exceptions to the Governing Body.
Maintain separate accounts and ledgers, reconcile monthly, and keep receipts.
Support the person's money skills, record transactions the same day, protect belongings, and report any loss.
Direct their money as able, review ledgers and inventories, and consent to any funds held.

documentation: Assessment of money-management ability
Signed authorization to hold funds
Individual ledgers, receipts and bank statements
Monthly reconciliation signed by a second person
Written confirmation from DODD and the county board for any room-and-board charge
Belongings and negotiable-item inventories
Loss or misuse incident reports
Final accounting and receipt at move-out or death
Quarterly compliance review notes

policies.title: Medicaid Provider Agreement, HCBS Approval and Service Boundaries (HPC and Shared Living)
policies.applies_to: Governing Body, Administrator, billing and compliance staff, and all staff who deliver or schedule HPC or Shared Living
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] delivers Individual Options (IO) waiver Homemaker/Personal Care (HPC) and Shared Living only with the required approvals, license and Medicaid agreement, and within the boundaries each service allows.
policies.policy: DODD operates the Individual Options waiver under an interagency agreement with ODM (OAC 5160-40-01, C50). If [AGENCY NAME] delivers HCBS in the facility, it submits the DODD application for approval, keeps an ODM Medicaid provider agreement, and follows the Chapter 5123-9 rule for each service delivered (OAC 5123-3-01(C)(3), C5). HPC is delivered only by a provider with an ODM Medicaid provider agreement, and a licensed provider keeps both its ORC 5123.19 license and the Medicaid agreement; noncompliance can lead to license or certification action (OAC 5123-9-30(C), C42). As an agency provider, [AGENCY NAME] maintains the general liability insurance of at least $1,000,000 and the proof of an unencumbered $10,000 line of credit or bank balance required for certification (OAC 5123-2-08, C49). Shared Living is a distinct service under OAC 5123-9-33 (C48): no more than 4 persons with a developmental disability may live in a home where it is delivered, a group of two is paid at 85% of the daily rate, and it is never combined with HPC for the same individual. HPC and money management are also never provided to the same individual. The agency does not start or bill any HCBS before every approval is in place. This policy supports the federal HCBS requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Homemaker/Personal Care, an IO waiver service delivered under OAC 5123-9-30.
An IO waiver service under OAC 5123-9-33 in which a person lives with a paid provider in a shared home, billed as a daily rate and distinct from HPC.
The agreement with the Ohio Department of Medicaid that allows a provider to bill Medicaid.

ODM's pause on new Medicaid enrollment applications for certain provider types, including waiver organizations, shown in the ODM notice effective 5/14/2026 through 11/14/2026 and subject to extension.

procedures: Before offering any HCBS, the Governing Body decides in writing which services [AGENCY NAME] will deliver (HPC, Shared Living, or both) and records that decision in the minutes (GOV-01).

The Administrator checks the ODM moratorium page before any new enrollment application is submitted. The notice effective 5/14/2026 through 11/14/2026 may apply to waiver individuals and organizations and may be extended. The Administrator confirms with ODM, in writing, whether it applies to [AGENCY NAME], and files the answer.

The Administrator submits the DODD application for approval of HCBS delivered in the facility and tracks the application until approved. No HCBS is delivered or billed before written approval is received.
The Administrator confirms the ODM Medicaid provider agreement is active, with the Medicaid provider number on file, and puts the expiration or revalidation dates on the compliance calendar.

The Administrator keeps the ORC 5123.19 license current (GOV-02). If the license lapses, is suspended or is revoked, or the Medicaid agreement ends, all billing for the affected service stops that day and the Governing Body is told within 1 business day.

The compliance officer keeps on file the certificate of general liability insurance of at least $1,000,000 and proof of an unencumbered $10,000 line of credit or bank balance, and renews them before they expire (GOV-03).
For each person, the Administrator confirms an ISP from the county board SSA authorizes the specific service before it starts. Services not on the ISP are not provided or billed.

Before accepting a person for HPC, the Administrator confirms in writing that the person does not also receive money management or Shared Living from [AGENCY NAME], and records the check in the admission file.

Before accepting a person for Shared Living, the Administrator confirms that the person does not receive HPC from the agency, and that the home will have no more than 4 persons with a developmental disability living in it, counting everyone with a developmental disability whether or not they receive Shared Living.

If a person's authorized services change in a way that would combine HPC with Shared Living or money management, the Administrator ends one service with the county board, in writing, before billing continues for both. Combined billing is never submitted.

For a Shared Living group of two, billing staff apply the 85% daily rate. The Administrator keeps a household roster showing the number of persons with a developmental disability in each Shared Living home and reviews it each quarter.
Staff are trained at hire and annually on the difference between HPC and Shared Living and on what each service may not include (ST-04).

If the Administrator learns DODD or ODM has taken action against the license, certification or agreement, or has been notified of noncompliance, the Administrator notifies the Governing Body within 1 business day and follows GOV-04.

The compliance officer reviews approvals, agreements, insurance, line of credit and service boundaries every quarter as part of the Internal Compliance Program and reports exceptions to the Governing Body (IC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Decides which HCBS to offer, ensures resources and insurance are in place, and acts on compliance exceptions.
Submits applications, confirms approvals and agreements, applies service boundaries at admission, and notifies the Governing Body of any adverse action.
Track agreement, insurance and line-of-credit dates, apply the correct rates, and block billing that crosses service boundaries.
Authorizes services on the ISP and coordinates changes.

policies.title: HPC Service Delivery, ISP Implementation and Documentation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, scheduling staff, and all direct support professionals delivering HPC
policies.purpose: To make sure every HPC service is delivered according to the ISP, covered when staff are absent, and documented in the way Ohio requires so it can support billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers HPC only according to an ISP developed under OAC 5123-4-02 (OAC 5123-9-30(D), C43). The county board SSA coordinates assessment and develops the ISP; the agency takes part in planning and carries out the plan (OAC 5123-3-03(C)-(E), C21). The agency arranges approved substitute coverage when scheduled staff are absent. No HPC is provided to a person who also receives money management or Shared Living from the agency. Each HPC service is documented with the content required by OAC 5123-9-30(E) (C44). On-site/on-call applies only when the individual is expected to be asleep at least 5 continuous hours and the provider is present and available but need not stay awake, and it may not be authorized in the provider's own residence (OAC 5123-9-30(B)(20), C46). As an agency provider, [AGENCY NAME] keeps a documented overtime review process (C43). This policy supports 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: Individual Service Plan developed under OAC 5123-4-02 with the individual, guardian, SSA and team.
A staff member who meets all qualification, background check and training requirements and who is approved by the agency to cover a scheduled HPC shift.
HPC authorized for a person expected to sleep at least 5 continuous hours, where the provider is present and available but need not stay awake.
The number of individuals one staff member serves at the same time during a unit of HPC.
A 15-minute billing unit of HPC.

procedures: Before the first HPC visit, the Administrator obtains the current ISP and confirms HPC is authorized, including the amount, frequency and any limits on location or tasks. A copy is placed in the service record (RC-01).
The Administrator and supervisor build a written service schedule from the ISP outcomes and shares it with the individual, guardian and assigned DSPs before the service starts.
Each DSP is oriented to the person's ISP, preferences, health and safety needs, and communication methods before working alone with the person (ST-04), and the orientation is signed and dated.
During each visit, the DSP delivers only the supports described in the ISP, in the manner the person prefers, and supports the person's choices and community integration (MP-01).
The DSP documents each service contemporaneously, before leaving or before the end of the shift. The note shows the type of service, date, and place of service.
The note records the individual's name and Medicaid ID, the provider's name and contract number, and the DSP's signature or initials.

The note records the group size (number of individuals served by that staff at the time), a description of what was done that ties to ISP outcomes, the units or time delivered, and the start and stop times.
Notes are written in plain factual language. Copy-and-paste or pre-filled notes, and notes written for services that were not delivered, are prohibited. Staff may not sign for another person.
Corrections are made by a single line through the error with initials and date. Late entries are labeled as late entries with the real date and reason.

If scheduled staff cannot work, the DSP notifies the supervisor as soon as possible. The supervisor assigns an approved substitute who meets all requirements and tells the person. The substitute's name is recorded in the visit note.

If no approved substitute is available, the supervisor tells the person and the SSA the same day, records the missed service, and does not bill for it. Staff who do not meet requirements, or who are unapproved, are never used to cover.

On-site/on-call is used only if the ISP and authorization allow it and the person is expected to sleep at least 5 continuous hours. The Administrator checks that the arrangement is not in the provider's own residence before it begins and documents the check.

For on-site/on-call, the DSP stays on the premises and available through the night, and documents any time the person woke and needed help. If the person needs awake support, the supervisor reviews whether the authorization and schedule still fit the person's needs and contacts the SSA.

Each pay period, the payroll lead identifies every employee who worked more than 40 hours in a week and any projected overtime. The Administrator documents a review of why overtime was needed, whether it was authorized in advance, whether the person's needs or schedule can be met without it, and the decision (PS-02).

The supervisor reviews a sample of notes weekly for completeness against the required elements, and the Administrator reviews notes before billing (HCBS-03). Missing elements are corrected before any claim is submitted.
Each quarter, the Administrator compares notes with the ISP outcomes and reports to the person, guardian and SSA on progress. Changes in need are sent to the SSA for an ISP update.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms authorization and ISP, approves substitutes and on-site/on-call arrangements, performs overtime review, and reviews notes before billing.
Builds schedules, arranges substitutes, reviews notes weekly, and corrects documentation errors.
Delivers only ISP-based supports, documents each visit contemporaneously with all required elements, and reports absences and changes in need.
Develops and updates the ISP and authorizes the service.

documentation: Current ISP and service authorization
Written service schedule
DSP orientation record
Visit notes with all required elements
Substitute coverage records
On-site/on-call eligibility check
Overtime review documentation
Weekly note audit results
Quarterly ISP progress reports

policies.title: EVV, Billing and Rate Rules
policies.applies_to: Administrator, billing and compliance staff, supervisors, and all direct support professionals delivering HPC
policies.purpose: To make sure all HPC claims are supported by Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) and complete documentation, billed in the correct units and at the correct rate, and submitted on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses EVV for HPC billed in 15-minute units (OAC 5123-9-30(D), C43), as required by 42 USC 1396b(l). On-site/on-call is excluded. Every claim must match an EVV visit. The agency uses Sandata, which ODM provides at no cost. HPC is billed in 15-minute units, up to 16 hours (64 units) per day, by assessed need, and claims are submitted within 350 days of service. Group-size rates follow OAC 5123-9-30(F)(3) (C45): when one staff serves two individuals the base rate is 107% of the one-to-one rate, for three individuals 117%, and for four or more 130%; the rate is divided among those served. Rates follow the county cost-of-doing-business category, and billing staff use the current appendix B table. Billing is allowed only while the agency holds the ORC 5123.19 license and the Medicaid provider agreement (OAC 5123-9-30(C), C42). The agency does not bill for services not delivered, not documented, not on the ISP, or delivered by unqualified staff. Federal rules on Medicaid provider enrollment, including 42 CFR 455.470 and any ODM enrollment moratorium, affect new enrollments only, and are tracked under HCBS-01.

definitions.definition: Electronic Visit Verification, an electronic record of the service type, individual, provider, date, and start and end times of a visit.
The EVV system provided by ODM at no cost to providers.
A 15-minute unit of HPC for billing.
The county cost-of-doing-business grouping that sets the HPC payment rate for the county where the service is delivered.
The DODD rate schedule table used to look up current HPC rates.

procedures: Before any HPC billing, the Administrator confirms the ODM Medicaid provider agreement is active and the ORC 5123.19 license is current (HCBS-01), and that the person's authorization and ISP cover the service.
The Administrator sets up Sandata accounts for the agency and assigns each DSP an ID and training. DSPs may not use another person's login.
At each visit, the DSP checks in at the start and checks out at the end using the approved EVV method. The visit is recorded against the correct individual, service and place of service.
On-site/on-call hours are not recorded in EVV and are billed under their own rules after the Administrator has confirmed the eligibility check described in HCBS-02.

If EVV cannot be completed because of a device or system problem, the DSP tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor enters a manual correction in the EVV system with the reason, using only the process allowed by ODM, and keeps the supporting record. Corrections are never made to increase billable time.
Billing staff match every claim line to an EVV visit and to a complete service note (HCBS-02) before submission. Any claim that does not match is held and corrected, or not billed.
Billing staff calculate units in 15-minute increments based on actual time delivered. A claim may not exceed 64 units (16 hours) in a day or the amount authorized for that person.

When one staff member serves more than one individual at the same time, the DSP records the group size, and billing applies the group-size rate: 107% of the one-to-one rate for two, 117% for three and 130% for four or more, with the rate divided among those served. Billing staff do not bill the full one-to-one rate for each person.

Billing staff look up the rate in the current appendix B table using the county's cost-of-doing-business category and the agency provider table, and record the table version used. They do not use rates from older tables or from independent provider tables.

Claims are submitted at least weekly, and no later than 30 days after the service date. No claim may be submitted later than 350 days after service. The compliance officer runs a monthly report of unbilled visits older than 60 days and resolves them.

Billing staff do not bill for missed visits, unapproved substitutes, training time, travel not allowed by rule, or time when the person was not present. They do not bill HPC for anyone who also receives Shared Living or money management from the agency.
The Administrator reviews each billing batch before submission and signs the review. Overtime is checked against the documented review required by HCBS-02.

When a denial, recoupment, or repayment request arrives, the compliance officer logs it within 2 business days, investigates the cause, corrects the root problem and refunds any overpayment found, and reports the matter to the Administrator and Governing Body.
If the agency finds that it billed in error, it corrects the claim or repays the overpayment promptly and documents the correction (IC-01).

The compliance officer reviews ODM's current EVV rule and any changes to GPS or location-capture requirements, and DODD and ODM notices about rates, at least once a year and when notified, and updates this policy and staff training. DODD has stated it does not expect rate changes before July 2027; the agency continues to use the current table until a new one is published.
Each quarter, the compliance officer audits a sample of claims against EVV records, notes, authorizations and rates, and reports results and corrective actions to the Governing Body (IC-01, MP-02).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms license and agreement status, signs each batch review, and oversees corrections and repayments.
Match claims to EVV and notes, apply correct units and rates, submit on time, and hold claims that do not match.
Runs unbilled-visit and quarterly claim audits, tracks denials and rule changes, and reports to the Governing Body.
Use EVV correctly for every visit, record group size accurately, and report system problems the same day.
Reviews audit results and requires corrective action.

documentation: EVV records and manual correction logs
Service notes matched to claims
Authorizations and ISPs
Rate table version used (appendix B) and CODB category
Signed batch reviews
Claim submission and denial logs
Refund and repayment records
Quarterly claim audit reports
Annual EVV and rate rule review

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support and Restrictive Interventions
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contractors serving individuals in the DODD-licensed residential facility and under the IO waiver (Homemaker/Personal Care and Shared Living)
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals with positive, person-centered strategies, uses restrictive measures only as a documented last resort, never uses prohibited measures, and honors the individual's rights and the HCBS settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses positive measures first. Our staff teach skills, change environments, honor preferences and respond to the function of behavior before any restrictive measure is considered. Under OAC 5123-2-06(C)(14), the following are never used: prone restraint; any restraint that restricts breathing or causes pain; disabling a communication device; denying meals; placing a person in a dark room; painful sound; shock; humiliating treatment; and any restrictive measure used as punishment or for staff convenience. Chemical restraint, manual restraint, mechanical restraint, rights restriction and time-out are last resorts. They are used only when there is a risk of harm (for a rights restriction, risk of harm or legal sanction), and only after the requirements of OAC 5123-2-06(D) are met. Time-out never exceeds 30 minutes per incident or 1 hour in 24 hours, is never behind a key-locked door, and is under constant visual supervision. Any behavior support that is not approved under this policy is a Category C Major Unusual Incident (MUI) and is reported under BP-03. Any restriction of a right also follows IR-02 and the HCBS settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4).

definitions.definition: Strategies that teach, reinforce and accommodate, such as environmental changes, skill building, choice-making, communication supports and reinforcement, and that do not restrict rights or movement.
A chemical, manual or mechanical restraint, a rights restriction or a time-out, each used only under this policy and OAC 5123-2-06.
Removal of an individual to a separate space for a limited period for risk of harm, subject to the time limits and supervision rules in this policy.
A written plan, authored by a qualified person, describing positive measures and any approved restrictive measure.
The committee that reviews and approves any strategy that includes a restrictive measure before it is used.
Any restrictive measure used without a current approved strategy, or any prohibited measure. It is a Category C MUI.

procedures: Before and at admission, the Administrator or designee and the individual's team review the individual's ISP and any existing behavioral support strategy so that staff know them before serving the person (see MP-01 and SS-01).
All staff are trained before working alone on positive behavior support, the list of prohibited measures, de-escalation and the MUI reporting duty. Training is recorded under ST-04.

Staff first respond to behavior with positive measures: offer choices, change the environment, give space, use the person's communication method, address unmet needs such as pain, hunger or fatigue, and follow the ISP.
Staff record behavior concerns on the behavior/incident log on the day they occur. The Administrator reviews the logs weekly for patterns.
If positive measures are not working, the Administrator asks the team (the individual, guardian if any, county board service coordinator, clinicians) to meet and assess the behavior.

No restrictive measure is proposed unless there is a risk of harm to the person or others (or, for a rights restriction, a legal sanction), and the team has documented that positive measures were tried and did not work.
A functional assessment must be completed within the 12 months before a restrictive measure is used. The Administrator verifies the assessment date before approving any restrictive strategy.
The behavioral support strategy is written by a qualified author. The author's name and credentials are recorded on the strategy.
Informed consent is obtained in writing from the individual or the guardian before the strategy is implemented. The consent form is filed in the service record (RC-01).
The strategy is submitted to the human rights committee. No restrictive measure is used until the committee has approved it in writing.
The strategy states how and when the guardian will be notified of any use of a restrictive measure. Staff follow those notification terms exactly.

When a time-out is used, the staff member keeps the person in constant visual supervision, never locks the door with a key, ends the time-out at 30 minutes at the latest, and tracks total time so the 1-hour-per-24-hours limit is not exceeded.

Any use of a restraint or time-out is documented the same shift: date, time, duration, antecedent, positive measures tried, measure used, staff involved, injuries, and the person's condition afterward. The Administrator reviews the record within one working day.

If a prohibited measure is used, or any restrictive measure is used without an approved strategy, staff report it immediately as an MUI under BP-03 (Category C, and Category A if abuse or neglect is suspected), and the staff member is removed from direct contact pending review.

The Administrator convenes the team to review each strategy at least every 90 days, reviewing data on use, injuries, effectiveness and whether the measure can be reduced or ended. The review is documented and sent to the human rights committee and guardian.
Any rights restriction is also handled under IR-02 (due process), and is limited in time and scope, and documented in the ISP.
The Administrator reviews all restrictive measure use quarterly as part of internal monitoring (MP-02 and IC-01) and corrects any problem found.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure no prohibited measure is used; verify assessment, consent and committee approval before any restrictive measure; track the 90-day reviews; report unapproved use.
Use positive measures first; follow only approved strategies; never use prohibited measures; document and report every use.
Write the strategy based on a current assessment and review it with the team.
Review and approve or decline strategies that include restrictive measures.
Give or withhold informed consent and take part in reviews.

documentation: Behavioral support strategy with author's name and credentials
Assessment completed within 12 months
Written informed consent
Human rights committee approval
Restrictive measure use log (including time-out start/stop times)
90-day review records
Guardian notification records
MUI incident reports for unapproved behavior support
Staff training records

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, Direct Support Assistants and contractors of [AGENCY NAME], in the licensed residential facility and in HPC and Shared Living services
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation of individuals' property, and to make sure that every suspected or actual incident is reported at once, the individual is protected, and no one is punished for reporting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation. Every employee must immediately report any suspected or actual MUI to the provider's designee, the county board or the DODD hotline (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(1)). The agency immediately secures medical care for the individual and immediately removes any staff member alleged to have committed physical or sexual abuse from contact with individuals (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(5)). The agency notifies the county board within 4 hours of discovery of abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(7)-(8)). Abuse, neglect, exploitation and unexplained death are Category A MUIs (OAC 5123-17-02(C)). The agency checks the abuser registry (OAC 5123-17-03) before hire and gives each staff member the annual written notice of conduct leading to abuser registry placement and of the 14-day charge-reporting duty (OAC 5123-3-01(D)). Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited. Disclosures about abuse, neglect or domestic violence victims are made only as permitted by 45 CFR 164.512(c) and agency privacy policy RC-02.

definitions.definition: Physical, sexual or verbal abuse or misuse of restraint or seclusion, as defined in OAC Chapter 5123-17 and categorized as a Category A MUI.
Failure of a caretaker to provide goods or services needed to avoid risk of harm. It is a Category A MUI.
Unlawful or improper use of an individual or the individual's resources for another's profit or advantage.
Deliberate misplacement, exploitation or wrongful temporary or permanent use of an individual's belongings or money.
The person named by [AGENCY NAME] to receive immediate MUI reports: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]; backup: [BACKUP DESIGNEE], [PHONE].
The state registry of persons placed on the registry for abuse, neglect, misappropriation or exploitation, checked before hire.

procedures: Before hire, [AGENCY NAME] runs the required background check and checks the abuser registry (OAC 5123-17-03). The result is filed under MP-05 and ST-03. No one is hired or allowed to work alone if listed.

At hire, and each year after, every employee receives the written notice of conduct that leads to abuser registry placement and of the duty to report any criminal charge to the agency within 14 days. The signed notice is filed in the personnel record (ST-01).

All new staff are trained before working alone on recognizing abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation, on how to report, and on the no-retaliation rule. Training is repeated at least annually and recorded (ST-04).

The DODD hotline number [DODD HOTLINE NUMBER], the county board's 24-hour number [COUNTY BOARD NUMBER] and the designee's number are posted where staff and individuals can see them and are given to each individual and guardian.

Any employee who suspects or witnesses abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation reports immediately, by phone, to the designee, the county board or the DODD hotline. The employee does not wait to investigate or to tell a supervisor first.

If an individual is in immediate danger or needs medical care, staff call 911, stay with the individual and give first aid within their training. Staff preserve evidence by not cleaning or discarding clothing, items or the scene unless required for safety.

The Administrator or designee ensures that medical care is secured immediately and that the individual is safe. If the individual has no injury, a nurse or other qualified person still checks the individual's condition the same day.

If the allegation is of physical or sexual abuse, the Administrator immediately removes the accused staff member from all contact with individuals. Removal is not a finding of guilt; it is a protective step. Other allegations are assessed on the same day for similar protective steps.

The Administrator or designee notifies the county board within 4 hours of discovery of abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation, even if the facts are not yet confirmed, and gives the county board all information it requests.

The Administrator notifies law enforcement when a crime may have occurred, and notifies the guardian and legal representative as soon as possible unless the guardian is the accused. The notice is documented.
The incident report is completed and submitted by 3 p.m. on the next working day, containing the content required by BP-03.

[AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with the county board, DODD, law enforcement and any other investigator, makes staff and records available and keeps the accused staff away from individuals and witnesses.

No employee, volunteer or individual may be threatened, disciplined, have hours cut, or otherwise retaliated against for making a good-faith report. Any retaliation is itself misconduct and may lead to termination. The Administrator reviews the reporter's status at 30 days.

After the investigation, the Administrator adopts and documents all preventive actions the county board or DODD recommends, along with any additional agency actions (retraining, supervision changes, environmental changes). Substantiated findings lead to discipline up to termination and referral for registry placement as required.
The Administrator reviews all abuse, neglect and exploitation reports at least quarterly to find trends (location, shift, person, staff) and corrects them under MP-02 and IC-01.

Disclosures of protected health information about suspected abuse victims to authorized agencies follow 45 CFR 164.512(c) and RC-02. The minimum necessary information is disclosed and each disclosure is logged.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected or actual abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation immediately; protect the individual; cooperate with investigators.
Secure medical care; remove accused staff when physical or sexual abuse is alleged; notify the county board within 4 hours; file the incident report by 3 p.m. next working day; prevent retaliation.
Run registry checks; maintain annual notices and training records.
Review reports, trends and corrective actions and ensure the policy is followed.

documentation: Abuser registry check results
Signed annual staff notice (abuser registry conduct and 14-day reporting)
MUI incident reports
County board and law enforcement notification log with times
Removal-from-contact records
Investigation and corrective action records
Training records
Quarterly trend review

policies.title: Reportable Incidents, Investigations and Missing Person/Elopement
policies.applies_to: All staff and the Administrator, for all individuals served in the licensed residential facility and through HPC and Shared Living
policies.purpose: To ensure that every Major Unusual Incident (MUI) is reported immediately, in the correct category, to the county board within 4 hours where required, and in a complete written incident report by 3 p.m. the next working day, and that missing individuals are found quickly and safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports and documents all MUIs under OAC 5123-17-02. Category A MUIs are abuse, neglect, exploitation and unexplained death. Category B MUIs are suicide attempt, natural death, medical emergency, missing individual, peer-to-peer act and significant injury. Category C MUIs are law enforcement involvement, hospitalization and unapproved behavior support. Staff report immediately to the designee, the county board or the DODD hotline (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(1)). The county board is notified within 4 hours of discovery of abuse, neglect, exploitation, misappropriation, peer-to-peer acts, prohibited sexual relations, unexplained death or a media inquiry, and the incident report is submitted by 3 p.m. the next working day (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(7)-(8)). For individuals receiving round-the-clock waiver services, all MUIs are reported wherever they occur (OAC 5123-17-02(D)(2)-(4)); for other individuals, [AGENCY NAME] reports those types that must be reported wherever they occur and the others when the individual is being served by [AGENCY NAME]. A missing individual is a Category B MUI and is handled under the written missing-person response below.

definitions.definition: An incident of the types listed in Categories A, B and C of OAC 5123-17-02 that must be reported to the county board and DODD.
Abuse, neglect, exploitation, and unexplained death.
Suicide attempt, natural death, medical emergency, missing individual, peer-to-peer act and significant injury.
Law enforcement involvement, hospitalization and unapproved behavior support.
The time any employee first knows or reasonably suspects that an MUI has occurred; the 4-hour clock starts then.
An individual whose whereabouts are unknown and who is at risk, or who is absent contrary to the ISP or safety plan.
A day the provider's office is open, Monday through Friday except legal holidays.

procedures: Staff who see, hear of or suspect any MUI immediately make sure the individual is safe and call 911 if there is an emergency. They then report immediately to the designee ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]), the county board [COUNTY BOARD NUMBER] or the DODD hotline [DODD HOTLINE NUMBER].

The designee immediately secures medical care as needed and takes protective steps. If physical or sexual abuse is alleged against a staff member, the designee immediately removes that staff member from contact with individuals (BP-02).
The designee records the time of discovery and decides the MUI category (A, B or C) using the lists in this policy. If unsure, the designee reports the event to the county board and asks.

For abuse, neglect, exploitation, misappropriation, peer-to-peer acts, prohibited sexual relations, unexplained death or a media inquiry, the designee notifies the county board within 4 hours of discovery and records the time, name of the person contacted and the information given.

The designee decides whether the incident is reportable under the round-the-clock rule. For an individual receiving round-the-clock waiver services, all MUIs are reported wherever they occur, including in the community, at work, during a hospital stay or on a home visit.
The designee notifies the guardian or legal representative, the service coordinator and, where a crime may have occurred, law enforcement, and documents each notification.

The staff member with first-hand knowledge writes the incident report on the day of the event. It includes: the individual's name and address; date, time and location; a who/what/when/where description; injuries; immediate actions; persons involved; witness statements; notifications made; medical follow-up; and the author's signature.
Witness statements are collected the same day, signed and dated. Staff do not discuss the event with each other before writing statements.

The Administrator reviews the report for completeness and submits it by 3 p.m. on the next working day. If the report cannot be complete by then, the Administrator submits what is known and updates it as facts are learned.
The Administrator logs every MUI in the MUI log (date, category, county board notification time, report submission time, follow-up) and keeps a copy in the individual's record (RC-01).

The Administrator cooperates with the county board's and DODD's investigation, provides records and staff, and implements the preventive measures recommended. Corrective actions are documented with a completion date.
Within 5 working days of each MUI, the Administrator confirms medical follow-up, ISP or health plan changes and staff retraining needs, and documents them.

MISSING PERSON/ELOPEMENT: When staff cannot find an individual, they immediately search the home, grounds and the individual's known locations for a short, defined period, and keep other individuals supervised. If the person is not found quickly, or is at risk of harm at any point, staff call 911 right away without waiting for a supervisor.

Staff give police the individual's description, photo, clothing, medications, health and communication needs, risks (traffic, water, weather) and places the person is known to go, and notify the designee immediately.

The designee organizes a continued search, calls the guardian and the county board (within 4 hours at the latest, and sooner as practical), and reports the event as a Category B MUI. The designee remains available to police until the person is found.

When the individual is found, staff arrange a medical check at once, return the person safely, and notify police, guardian and county board. The Administrator reviews the elopement risk in the ISP and updates the individual's safety plan, supervision level and environmental safeguards, and retrains staff as needed.
Monthly, the Administrator reviews MUI trends (type, time, location, staff, individual) and reports the results to the governing body under MP-02 and IC-01.

Assign the category; notify the county board within 4 hours when required; submit the incident report by 3 p.m. next working day; run the missing-person response; track corrective actions.
Assess injury or medical emergency and document follow-up (HC-04).
Review MUI trends and ensure resources for prevention.
