policies.title: Residential Environment and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: The licensed residential facility at [ADDRESS] and any home where [AGENCY NAME] provides services, to the extent it controls the setting
policies.purpose: To keep the home accessible, clean, safe and homelike, to meet the space and safety standards of OAC 5123-3-02, and to meet the Americans with Disabilities Act.
policies.policy: The home operated by [AGENCY NAME] is accessible, clean, safe and homelike (OAC 5123-3-02(C)-(E)). The home has an annual fire inspection and a carbon monoxide detector if it has a gas furnace or gas water heater. Each individual has at least 80 sq ft of living area. No more than 2 individuals share a bedroom (at least 80 sq ft for a single and 120 sq ft for a double). The home has at least 1 bathroom for each 4 individuals. Individuals have free access to a telephone. No signage identifies or labels individuals as residents of a program. The fire safety and emergency response plan is approved by state or local authority and shared with the county board; floor plans are posted; exits are kept clear; a fire extinguisher is on each floor; and a home of 5 or fewer individuals has smoke detectors on each floor (OAC 5123-3-02(F)(1)-(8)). The agency complies with the ADA, and confirms local zoning, building and occupancy approvals before the home is used and before changes in use.

definitions.definition: Space in the home that is available to individuals for daily living, measured at 80 sq ft or more per person under the licensing standard.
Furnished, decorated and run like a private home, not an institution, with personal items and choices honored.
Usable by individuals with physical, sensory or other disabilities, including entrances, routes, bathrooms and communication.

definitions.term: Fire safety and emergency response plan
definitions.definition: The written plan approved by state or local authority and shared with the county board (see FS-01).

procedures: Before the home is licensed or its use is changed, the Administrator confirms in writing with the local zoning, building and fire officials that zoning, building and occupancy approvals are in place, and files the approvals with the licensing records (GOV-02).

The Administrator measures each bedroom and living area and records the square footage on a room-by-room chart. Each individual must have at least 80 sq ft of living area, a single bedroom at least 80 sq ft, and a shared bedroom at least 120 sq ft with no more than 2 occupants.
The Administrator counts bathrooms against the number of individuals living in the home and confirms at least 1 bathroom for each 4 individuals. The count is rechecked at each admission.
The Administrator schedules the annual fire inspection with the local fire authority, keeps the inspection report, corrects any violation by the date set, and records the correction.
The Administrator identifies whether the home has a gas furnace or gas water heater. If so, a working carbon monoxide detector is installed and tested monthly. Test results are logged.
Smoke detectors are installed on each floor (required for facilities of 5 or fewer) and tested monthly. A fire extinguisher is placed on each floor, inspected monthly and serviced annually.
Floor plans showing exits are posted and exits and exit paths are kept clear at all times. Staff check exits at the start of each shift (see FS-01 and FS-03).

Staff complete a documented walk-through of the home weekly for hazards, cleanliness, repairs, lighting, hot water temperature, trip hazards and working equipment. The Administrator reviews the checklist and repairs hazards at once or protects individuals until the repair is made.
Staff clean the home on a written schedule so that bathrooms, kitchen, floors, bedding and common areas are clean, free of odors and in good repair. Infection control cleaning follows HE-02.

The Administrator assesses each individual's accessibility needs on admission and when needs change (ramps, grab bars, doorways, bathing, communication supports, visual or auditory alerts) and makes reasonable modifications consistent with the ADA. Needs and modifications are recorded in the individual's file.

Individuals have free access to a telephone at any time, in private, in a location of their choice, at no charge for local calls. Staff do not monitor calls except as stated in a rights restriction approved under IR-02.

The home is decorated and furnished with individuals' choices. Individuals can decorate and personalize their bedrooms. Staff remove any sign, label or notice identifying residents as clients or as having a disability from the exterior and the public areas of the home.
The Administrator reviews the environment at least quarterly during internal monitoring (MP-02) and asks individuals what they would like changed. Results and corrective actions are documented.

Before any renovation, change in bedroom use or change in the number of individuals, the Administrator confirms with the licensing agency and local authorities that the change meets standards, and updates the approved fire safety plan and posted floor plans.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain approvals, inspections and space standards; correct hazards; assess accessibility; ensure the plan and floor plans are current.
Do shift exit checks and cleaning; report hazards immediately; protect individuals' phone access and personal space.
Provide resources for repairs, modifications and inspections.
Choose furnishings, decoration and use of their space as they wish.

documentation: Zoning, building and occupancy approvals
Room-by-room square footage and bathroom ratio chart
Annual fire inspection reports and corrections
Smoke, carbon monoxide and extinguisher test and service logs
Weekly environment walk-through checklists
Accessibility assessments and modification records
Quarterly environmental review

policies.title: Infection Prevention, Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, Direct Support Assistants, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] who work in the home or with individuals
policies.purpose: To keep the home clean and safe, to prevent the spread of infection among individuals and staff, to meet OSHA bloodborne pathogens requirements, and to protect employee health information.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps the home clean and safe (OAC 5123-3-02(C)-(E)) and complies with applicable federal law, including worker-protection law (OAC 5123-3-01(C)(5)). The agency maintains an OSHA bloodborne pathogens exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030, offers hepatitis B vaccination to employees with occupational exposure, and trains staff. Staff use standard precautions, hand hygiene, and written cleaning and laundry procedures. Ill staff are excluded from direct contact according to written criteria. No Ohio rule specifying TB screening for staff was found in the sources reviewed for this manual; as agency policy, [AGENCY NAME] adopts the TB screening procedure below, and the Administrator will confirm DODD's expectations and update the procedure if DODD requires a different method or schedule. Employee health records are kept in a confidential file separate from the personnel file.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices used with every individual and every body fluid, including hand hygiene, gloves, safe handling of sharps and cleaning of surfaces.
The written OSHA plan identifying jobs with exposure to blood or other infectious material and describing protections, vaccination, training and post-exposure follow-up.
Contact with blood or other potentially infectious material that may result from performing an employee's duties.
A review of symptoms and risks and a test or other method chosen by the agency to identify tuberculosis infection.

procedures: The Administrator, with a nurse or other qualified consultant, writes the exposure control plan identifying jobs and tasks with exposure risk (for example, first aid, personal care, laundry, cleaning body fluids), and reviews the plan at least annually and when tasks change.

Before an employee with exposure risk starts the job, and annually afterward, the agency trains the employee on bloodborne pathogens, standard precautions, personal protective equipment, safe sharps handling, cleanup of spills and post-exposure steps. Training is recorded under ST-04.

The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccine, at no cost, to employees with occupational exposure, within the time required by 29 CFR 1910.1030. An employee who declines signs a declination form, and may later change their mind.
The agency keeps gloves, masks, disposable gowns, sharps containers, spill cleanup kits and hand-washing supplies in the home and checks stock weekly. Staff reorder before supplies run out.

Staff wash hands or use sanitizer before and after contact with an individual, before preparing or serving food, before and after giving medication, after toileting or personal care, and after glove removal.

Staff clean and disinfect bathrooms, kitchen surfaces, door handles and shared equipment on the written cleaning schedule. Soiled laundry is handled with gloves, washed separately in hot water as the plan states, and not carried against the body.
Sharps (such as lancets) go into a puncture-resistant sharps container and are disposed of per the exposure control plan and the law. Staff never recap needles by hand.

If a staff member is exposed to blood or body fluid, the staff member washes the area at once, reports to the Administrator immediately and is sent for medical evaluation as the plan provides, at no cost. The Administrator documents the exposure, source individual (with confidentiality) and follow-up on the same day.

TB screening: before starting work with individuals, each new employee, Direct Support Assistant and volunteer completes a symptom and risk screen and provides a TB test result or other documentation of TB status as selected by the agency's nurse consultant. The Administrator keeps the result in the employee health file.

The Administrator confirms with DODD or the county board the current expectation for TB screening and updates this procedure and the schedule for repeat screening when guidance changes. The date of that confirmation is recorded.

Staff who have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an undiagnosed rash, a sore that cannot be covered, or symptoms of a communicable disease, or who have been told to stay home by a health provider, must not work with individuals and must call the Administrator before the shift. Staff may return when they meet the written criteria in the exclusion list (for example, 24 hours without fever or vomiting, or provider clearance).

The Administrator uses a written exclusion list that identifies conditions, the time away from work and the clearance needed. The list is reviewed by a nurse consultant and given to every employee at hire.

When an individual has an infectious illness, staff follow the nurse's or physician's instructions on isolation, hygiene, cleaning and notification of the guardian and county board. Staff report suspected outbreaks (two or more people with similar symptoms) to the Administrator immediately, and the Administrator notifies the local health department as required by law.

Employee health records, including vaccination or declination forms, TB documentation, exposure reports and medical statements, are kept in a locked or access-controlled confidential file separate from the personnel file, and released only as the law permits.
The Administrator reviews infection incidents, exposures and staff illness at least quarterly in internal monitoring (MP-02), and corrects supply, training or procedure problems.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the exposure control plan, training, vaccination offers, TB screening records, exclusion list and confidential health files.
Review the plan, TB procedure and exclusion criteria; advise on outbreaks and exposures.
Use standard precautions, report exposures and illness, stay home when ill.
Fund supplies, vaccination and exposure follow-up.

documentation: Written exposure control plan with annual review date
Bloodborne pathogens training records
Hepatitis B vaccination or declination forms
TB screening documentation and date of confirmation with DODD
Exposure incident reports
Staff illness and exclusion records
Cleaning schedules and supply checks
Confidential employee health files, separate from personnel files

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, Direct Support Assistants, volunteers, contractors, the Administrator and the operator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set clear standards of conduct and professional boundaries that protect individuals' dignity, rights, money and safety, and to meet OAC 5123-3-04(D).
policies.policy: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] provide person-centered services, know the individual's ISP before serving, take reasonable steps to prevent incidents, and respect the rights listed in ORC 5123.62 (OAC 5123-3-04(D)). No staff member may be impaired by alcohol or drugs while on duty. A Direct Support Professional (DSP) may not serve their own minor child or spouse, or the administrator's minor child or spouse, as an individual. Staff must not financially exploit individuals, borrow money or property from them, give or receive personal gifts, or engage in any prohibited sexual relations with an individual; prohibited sexual relations are reportable as an MUI. A related guardian may be paid staff only after approval of the probate court, per DODD. Every staff member signs a code of conduct at hire and each year, and also receives the annual written notice about abuser registry conduct and the 14-day charge-reporting duty (OAC 5123-3-01(D)).

definitions.definition: The limit between the helping role of staff and the personal life of an individual, which protects the individual from exploitation or harm.
Under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs or misused medication so that the staff member's judgment, alertness or performance is affected.
Using an individual's money, property or benefits for staff or another person's gain, including loans, gifts, purchases and use of cards or accounts.
Sexual contact or sexual relationships between staff and an individual served, which are reportable as an MUI.
A guardian who is a family member of the individual and who may also be hired as paid staff.

procedures: At hire and each year afterward, each staff member reads and signs the code of conduct. It covers boundaries, impairment, gifts, money, sexual relations, confidentiality, social media, reporting duties and no-retaliation. Signed copies are filed in the personnel record (ST-03).
At orientation, before working alone, and annually, the agency trains staff on rights under ORC 5123.62, boundaries, person-centered service and the ISP. Training is recorded under ST-04.
Before serving an individual, the staff member reads the individual's ISP and any behavior support strategy and signs that they have done so. The Administrator confirms before the person works alone.

Staff must not report to work, or remain on duty, while impaired by alcohol or drugs, including misuse of prescription or over-the-counter medicines. A staff member who is on a prescribed medication that may affect performance tells the Administrator so duties can be adjusted.

If a supervisor reasonably suspects impairment, the supervisor immediately removes the staff member from duty, arranges safe transport (never allowing the staff member to drive), makes sure individuals are supervised, documents observed signs, and notifies the Administrator the same day.

The Administrator does not schedule any DSP to serve their own minor child or spouse, or the administrator's minor child or spouse, as an individual. The Administrator checks the staff schedule against the household and family information at hire and at each admission.

A family member who is a guardian is not hired as paid staff for the individual unless the probate court has approved the arrangement. The Administrator obtains and files the court approval, as DODD requires, before the person is paid, and rechecks at renewal.

Staff do not borrow or lend money, accept or give personal gifts, sell items to individuals, use an individual's money, cards, vehicle or property for themselves, or ask an individual for favors. Small gifts of nominal value on holidays are reported to the Administrator and logged.
Staff do not use individuals' personal information, photographs or stories on social media or elsewhere without written consent and agency approval, and keep information confidential (RC-02).

Staff do not enter into romantic, sexual or business relationships with an individual. Staff do not have sexual contact with an individual in any circumstance. Staff who learn of or suspect prohibited sexual relations report at once under BP-02 and BP-03, and the Administrator notifies the county board within 4 hours.
Staff do not discipline individuals, make threats or use humiliating, demeaning or abusive language. Staff use positive supports only as in BP-01.

Staff report any breach of this policy, by themselves or others, immediately to the Administrator or the DODD hotline [DODD HOTLINE NUMBER]. No staff member may be retaliated against for reporting in good faith.

Staff report any criminal charge against themselves to the Administrator within 14 days as described in the annual notice (ST-01), and the Administrator reviews the charge for effect on employment under MP-05.
The Administrator investigates each reported violation promptly and applies discipline up to termination. Serious violations are reported to the county board, DODD and law enforcement, as required.
Supervisors observe staff practice and review code-of-conduct compliance at least quarterly (MP-03), and the Administrator reports patterns to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Enforce the code of conduct; check scheduling for family relationships; obtain probate court approval for related guardians; investigate violations and report as required.
Observe staff, remove impaired staff from duty and document.
Follow the code of conduct, maintain boundaries, report violations and prohibited relations.
Approve this policy and review conduct trends.

documentation: Signed code of conduct at hire and annually
Signed ISP review statements
Annual abuser registry and 14-day reporting notice
Probate court approval for any related guardian paid as staff
Impairment observation and removal records
Gift log
Investigation and disciplinary records

policies.title: Wage and Hour, Payroll and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME] (direct support professionals, supervisors, support staff, administrative staff) in the DODD-licensed residential facility and in the DODD-certified Individual Options (IO) waiver Homemaker/Personal Care (HPC) and Shared Living services; the Administrator, payroll staff and the governing body.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee correctly and on time, stays current on payroll taxes, workers' compensation and unemployment premiums, and controls and documents overtime. The policy also ensures that wage and hour compliance supports, and never compromises, the staffing individuals need and the accuracy of Medicaid billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with Chapter 5123-3 and with applicable federal, state and local wage and hour, workers' compensation, unemployment and tax withholding laws (OAC 5123-3-01(C)(5)(a),(e),(f)). The agency stays current on payroll taxes, workers' compensation premiums and unemployment premiums (OAC 5123-3-01(D)(3)-(5)). Specifically: (1) Employees are paid at least the minimum wage that applies to the agency. For 2026 the Ohio non-tipped minimum wage is $11.00 per hour for covered employers, while employers grossing less than $405,000 follow the federal minimum. The Administrator confirms which rate applies each year against the current Ohio Department of Commerce poster. (2) Non-exempt employees are paid overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. The state overtime rule excludes employers grossing less than $150,000 per year, but the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) may still apply, so the agency applies the more protective rule that governs it. (3) As a third-party employer of direct care workers, the agency does not treat DSPs as exempt under the companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR 552). (4) As an agency HPC provider, the agency keeps a documented overtime review process (OAC 5123-9-30(D)). (5) Schedules are prepared in advance and available at each facility, staff on duty are scheduled by individuals' needs, and enough support staff are provided that DSPs are not pulled from primary duties (OAC 5123-3-01(D)(3)-(5)). Overtime is managed through planning and approved substitute coverage, never by unrecorded work. No employee is asked or allowed to work off the clock, and all hours worked are recorded and paid. The agency does not bill HPC for a person who receives Shared Living or money management from the agency for the same period (OAC 5123-9-30(D)).

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) set by [AGENCY NAME] in writing, used to calculate overtime. Hours are not averaged across workweeks.

All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including direct support, documentation, required training, staff meetings, required travel during the workday, and time on duty at the facility. Hours worked are determined under the FLSA.
An employee entitled to minimum wage and overtime. All DSPs and most support staff are non-exempt unless the Administrator documents that a specific exemption is met.
Hours worked over 40 in a workweek, paid at 1.5 times the employee's regular rate of pay.
The hourly rate used to compute overtime, including the base rate and any non-discretionary bonuses, shift differentials or similar pay required by law to be included.
The documented agency procedure in this policy by which projected and actual overtime is reviewed, approved or corrected, and used to improve scheduling and coverage (OAC 5123-9-30(D)).
Electronic Visit Verification, the system used to record HPC visits in 15-minute units (OAC 5123-9-30(D)).

procedures: Before the start of each calendar year, and whenever notified of a change, the Administrator checks the current Ohio Department of Commerce, Division of Industrial Compliance wage and hour poster (614-644-2239 for questions), determines which minimum wage applies to the agency based on gross receipts, and records the determination and date in the payroll compliance file.
The Administrator sets the agency's fixed workweek in writing and gives it to payroll. The workweek is not changed to avoid overtime.

At hire, payroll classifies each position as exempt or non-exempt in writing. DSPs, direct care staff and support staff are classified as non-exempt unless the Administrator documents the basis for an exemption. Companionship and live-in exemptions are not used for DSPs (29 CFR 552). The classification is filed in the personnel record (see ST-03).

Before any Shared Living provider or other worker is engaged as an independent provider or contractor instead of an employee, the Administrator documents a classification review under federal and Ohio law, and consults the agency's payroll advisor or counsel if the result is unclear. Workers are not labeled contractors simply to avoid wage and hour or tax obligations.

Each non-exempt employee records time worked daily, through the timekeeping system or EVV for HPC visits, and reviews and attests to the record at the end of each pay period. Supervisors do not alter time records except to correct a documented error, with the employee's knowledge and a written note of the reason.

Time spent in required orientation, training and competency checks (ST-04), staff meetings, drills (FS-03), required travel between individuals' locations during the workday, and documentation is counted as hours worked and paid.

The scheduler prepares staff schedules in advance, based on individuals' needs, and makes the current schedule available at each facility (ST-02). Schedules are built to keep projected hours at or below 40 per employee where possible.

Each workday, the payroll or scheduling designee runs the hours report. Each week, before the schedule is finalized, the designee flags any employee projected to exceed 40 hours and gives the list to the Administrator.

Overtime review: the Administrator or designee reviews each flagged employee, documents the reason (for example vacancy, call-off, change in an individual's needs, emergency), and decides whether to approve the overtime, reassign hours, or use approved substitute coverage. The decision and date are recorded on the weekly overtime review log.

Overtime is approved in advance wherever practicable. If an employee works overtime without prior approval, the employee is still paid for all hours worked at the overtime rate. The supervisor addresses any attendance, scheduling or authorization concern through supervision (MP-03) and never through reduced pay or unpaid time.

Employees are not asked or allowed to work off the clock, to clock out and keep working, or to "bank" hours across workweeks. Any employee who believes they were not paid for all time worked reports it to the Administrator, who investigates and corrects it promptly. Employees who report are protected from retaliation.

Each month, the Administrator reviews the overtime log for patterns (repeat overtime by the same employees, repeated coverage gaps, support staff shortages). If DSPs are being pulled from primary duties or covering repeated vacancies, the Administrator documents a corrective action such as hiring, adding support staff, cross-training or substitute coverage arrangements, consistent with OAC 5123-3-01(D)(3)-(5). The results are reported to the governing body at least quarterly (GOV-01).

Each pay period, before payroll is finalized, payroll reconciles hours paid to HPC for each individual against EVV records, the ISP-authorized units, and the daily limit by assessed need (see HCBS-03). Differences are resolved and documented. The agency does not bill HPC for any individual who receives Shared Living or money management from the agency for the same period (see HCBS-01).

Payroll withholds and remits federal, Ohio and local taxes on schedule, and pays unemployment and workers' compensation premiums when due. The Administrator confirms monthly that all accounts are current, and keeps proof of payment and current workers' compensation and unemployment coverage in the compliance file. Any notice of delinquency or audit is given to the Administrator the same day.

Pay statements show hours worked, the regular and overtime rates, gross and net pay and deductions. Employees are paid on regular, scheduled paydays. Any pay error is corrected in the next pay period, or sooner if the underpayment is significant, and the correction is documented.

Payroll and time records are kept for at least three years, or longer if required by RC-03 or by another law, and are available for inspection by DODD, the Ohio Department of Commerce, the U.S. Department of Labor and other authorized agencies.
The agency reviews this policy annually, and whenever minimum wage, overtime rules or DODD rule changes occur. Changes are made with the governing body and the Administrator.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the agency has funds and systems to meet payroll, tax and premium obligations, and reviews the overtime reports at least quarterly.

Determines the applicable minimum wage, classifies positions and workers, approves or redirects overtime, runs the overtime review process, confirms tax and premium accounts are current, and investigates pay complaints.
Processes payroll accurately and on time, applies overtime rules, reconciles payroll with EVV and authorized units, remits taxes and premiums, and maintains payroll records.
Prepare schedules in advance, post them at each facility, flag projected overtime, arrange approved substitute coverage, and make sure time records are complete and accurate.

responsibilities.role: Direct Support Professionals and other non-exempt staff
responsibilities.duty: Record all time worked accurately, do not work off the clock, obtain approval before overtime when practicable, and report any pay discrepancy to the Administrator.

documentation: Annual minimum wage determination and Ohio wage and hour poster confirmation
Written workweek definition and position classification (exempt/non-exempt) records
Worker classification reviews for any independent provider or contractor
Employee time records and attestation of hours each pay period
Weekly overtime review log showing flagged employees, reasons, decisions and dates
Monthly overtime pattern review and corrective actions, and quarterly governing body reports
Payroll-to-EVV and authorized-units reconciliation records
Pay statements, payroll registers and corrections
Proof of payment of payroll taxes, workers' compensation and unemployment premiums, and current coverage certificates
Payroll and time records retained for at least three years (see RC-03)

required_items.text: Written policies and procedures that address management practices regarding: Person-centered planning and self-determination;
Individuals' satisfaction with services delivered;
Internal monitoring and evaluation procedures to improve services delivered;
Supervision of staff;
The training plan described in paragraph (D)(7) of this rule;
Service delivery;
Background investigations for employment in accordance with rule 5123-2-02 of the Administrative Code; and
Volunteers (when the residential facility engages volunteers).
Demonstrate an established internal compliance program to ensure compliance with requirements for: Residential facilities in accordance with rules in Chapter 5123-3 of the Administrative Code;

Background investigations and appropriate actions in accordance with rule 5123-2-02 of the Administrative Code, for its administrator, licensee, operator, supervisors of direct support professionals, direct support professionals, direct support assistants, and volunteers;

Service delivery, service documentation, and billing for services in accordance with Chapter 5123. of the Revised Code and rules adopted pursuant to that chapter for supported living services and the specific home and community-based services provided; and
Management of individuals' funds.
Ensure the operator and its employees interact with individuals in a way to safeguard the rights of individuals enumerated in sections 5123.62 and 5123.65 of the Revised Code.
Meet the requirements established under sections 5123.63 and 5123.64 of the Revised Code.

Annually notify in writing each of its staff members explaining the conduct for which the staff member may be placed on the abuser registry, and set forth the requirement for supervisors of direct support professionals, direct support professionals and direct support assistants to report in writing to the operator, within fourteen calendar days, a formal charge, conviction, guilty plea, or finding of eligibility for intervention in lieu of conviction for the offenses listed in divisions (A)(3)(a) to (A)(3)(e) of section 109.572 of the Revised Code.
Ensure that staff are on duty on the basis of the needs of individuals being served. Staff schedules will be prepared in advance and available for review at each residential facility.
Maintain personnel records for each employee in accordance with the residential facility's personnel policies.

Develop and implement a written training plan for its administrator, supervisors of direct support professionals, direct support professionals, direct support assistants, support staff, and volunteers that:
Is consistent with the needs of individuals served, best practice, and the requirements set forth in appendix A, appendix B, appendix C, and appendix D to this rule.
Describes the method (e.g., written test, skills demonstration, or documented observation by supervisor) that will be used to establish competency in areas of training.
Is updated at least once every twelve months and identifies who is responsible for arranging or providing the training and projected timelines for completion of the training.

Maintain a written record of training completed by the administrator, supervisors of direct support professionals, direct support professionals, direct support assistants, support staff, and volunteers that includes a description of the training completed, the date of training, the duration of training, and when applicable, the instructor's name.
An operator will designate in writing a staff member to whom executive authority has been delegated in the temporary absence of the administrator.

When the administrator leaves a residential facility's employ, the operator will provide the operator's plan for identifying a new administrator and identify the person to whom executive authority has been delegated in the interim period.

A person employed as a direct support assistant will not, under any circumstances: (a) provide intimate personal care; (b) operate a vehicle to transport an individual; (c) administer medication or perform health-related activities; (d) provide any care or perform any task expressly forbidden by the individual; or (e) implement any restrictive measure as defined in rule 5123-2-06.

Volunteer requirements (applies when the facility uses volunteers): volunteers are under supervision of paid supervisory staff at all times; volunteers do not provide intimate personal care, administer medication, or perform health-related activities; volunteers who provide more than forty hours of direct service per calendar year complete appendix D training and a background investigation at least once every five years; and the operator will not engage a volunteer who is on the listed databases or who has a disqualifying conviction within the exclusionary period.

Each residential facility will have a fire safety and emergency response plan approved by the state/local authority that at a minimum, addresses the actions to be taken in the event of a fire, tornado, or other natural disaster.
A policy that addresses smoking regulations and the storage of combustible materials;
A fire safety training program that includes provisions for rescue, alarm, containment, and evacuation;
Designation of a tornado shelter or safe area in the residential facility and the procedure for accessing the area;
Responses to fires, weather-related emergencies, or other disasters when relocation of individuals is not required;

Responses to fires, weather-related emergencies, or other disasters when relocation of individuals is required, including designation of a pre-arranged place to meet in case of a physical evacuation of the residential facility; and
A procedure for permitting re-entry to the residential facility following a fire safety drill and/or physical evacuation.
The residential facility will share the fire safety and emergency response plan with the county board of developmental disabilities.

A current graphic floor plan will be posted unobstructed on each floor and in an area most appropriate for the posting of staff information, including: (a) primary and secondary means of exit from each floor; (b) location of pull stations and fire control system panels, when applicable; (c) fire escapes; (d) telephone number of the local fire department or 911; (e) designated tornado shelter or safe area; and (f) designated meeting places in case of fire.

The operator shall conduct and document at least three fire safety drills in a twelve-month period with one conducted during the morning, one conducted during the afternoon or evening, and one conducted during the time when individuals are routinely asleep.
The operator shall conduct and document at least one tornado drill in a twelve-month period.
Fire safety drills and tornado drills may be announced or unannounced and will be conducted in accordance with the assessed needs of individuals as identified in their individual service plans.

Residential facility staff will be trained in fire safety, operation of fire safety equipment and warning systems, and the residential facility's fire safety and emergency response plan in accordance with rule 5123-3-01.

Each individual will participate in documented training of the fire safety and emergency response plan within thirty calendar days of residency and at least once during every twelve-month period thereafter, appropriate to the individual's needs based on assessment.

Except at an ICF/IID, individuals may be trained to assist one another in case of fire or other emergency to the extent their abilities permit without additional personal risk and as indicated in their individual service plans.
Report to the department within one business day any fire to which a local fire department responded.
Notify each individual's family member or guardian, as applicable, as soon as possible when an emergency requires the operator to relocate individuals from the residential facility.
Report to the department and the county department of job and family services within one business day when an emergency requires the operator to relocate individuals.
Provide weekly updates to the department about individuals who have been relocated due to an emergency until the individuals return or permanently relocate.

Admission of residents - an operator shall: (a) admit as residents only individuals whose service needs can be met by the residential facility; (b) when reviewing an application for admission, consider its ability to maintain adequate services to all residents; (c) notify the individual and referring party in writing of the admission decision within thirty calendar days of receiving an application and referral information; (d) notify the county board in writing within fourteen calendar days of admitting a new resident, after securing informed consent to provide the notification. (C)(1): Admission to a residential facility is voluntary, requiring informed consent.

Standards of service provision - the operator, administrator, and staff shall: (a) provide services in a person-centered manner; (b) be able to effectively communicate with each individual; (c) be knowledgeable in the individual service plan before providing services; (d) implement services in accordance with the individual service plan; (e) take all reasonable steps to prevent the occurrence or recurrence of major unusual incidents and unusual incidents; (f) comply with rule 5123-2-06 regarding behavioral support strategies.

An operator shall ensure that a direct support professional does not: (a) provide services to the DSP's minor child; (b) provide services to the DSP's spouse; (c) provide services to the minor child of the administrator; (d) provide services to the spouse of the administrator; (e) administer medication or perform health-related activities unless the DSP meets the applicable requirements of Chapters 4723., 5123., and 5126. of the Revised Code; (f) use or be under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs, illegal chemical substances, or controlled substances that may adversely affect the ability to furnish services while providing services.
Self-administration or assistance with self-administration of prescribed medication will be conducted in accordance with rule 5123:2-6-02 of the Administrative Code.
Delegation of nursing tasks, excluding the provision of health-related activities, will be conducted in accordance with rule 5123-6-06 and Chapter 4723-13 of the Administrative Code.
Administration of prescribed medication pursuant to sections 5123.42 to 5123.46 of the Revised Code will be conducted in accordance with Chapters 5123-6 and 5123:2-6 of the Administrative Code.
An operator will comply with the requirements for reporting medication/treatment errors in accordance with rules 5123-6-07 and 5123-17-02 of the Administrative Code.

An operator shall develop and implement written procedures for the disposal of prescribed medication which require: (a) disposal of prescribed medication to be verified and recorded by two staff members or by an independent external entity; (b) dangerous drugs to be disposed in accordance with rule 4729-9-06 of the Administrative Code.

In the event of termination of services pursuant to rule 5123-3-05, an operator shall ensure: (a) a written accounting of prescribed medication is completed no later than the last day of residency and verified by two staff members; (b) a plan is developed for transfer of prescribed medication to the individual or guardian.

In the event of the death of an individual, an operator shall ensure: (a) a written accounting of prescribed medication is completed immediately and no later than twenty-four hours following the death and verified by two staff members; (b) the operator and staff cooperate with any investigation by a legally authorized entity; (c) disposal of prescribed medication occurs in accordance with the written procedures in (E)(5), unless an investigation calls for the disposal to be delayed.

Transportation - an operator shall: (1) provide or arrange for transportation in accordance with each resident's individual service plan; (2) ensure each employee providing transportation holds a valid driver's license; (3) ensure each such employee is covered by valid personal or corporate liability insurance as specified in Ohio law; (4) obtain a BMV driving record for each such employee no earlier than fourteen calendar days before initial employment as a driver and at least once every three years thereafter (six or more points prohibits providing transportation); (5) require each such employee to immediately notify the operator in writing if the employee accumulates six or more points or the license is suspended or revoked.
Develop and implement written policies and procedures regarding vehicle accessibility, vehicle maintenance, and requirements for vehicle drivers.
An operator shall offer daily meals and snacks that meet an individual's nutritional needs and preferences as identified by the individual.

Modified texture or therapeutic diets shall be prepared and served in accordance with the instructions of a physician or licensed dietitian. An operator shall maintain instructions regarding modified texture or therapeutic diets in accordance with paragraph (J).

Meals shall provide for variety, substitutions, and accommodation of individuals' personal preferences and religious beliefs. Individuals shall participate in meal planning and preparation to the extent of their interest and ability.
Fresh food supplies sufficient for three days and staple food supplies sufficient for at least five days shall be available in the residential facility at all times.

Food shall be prepared and stored properly and in accordance with health codes to protect it against contamination and spoilage. Food products shall be stored separately from potentially harmful non-food items, particularly cleaning and laundry compounds.

Clothing - an operator shall ensure each individual has an adequate amount of personal clothing in good repair, well-fitting, and comparable in style to that worn by age peers in the community (the team ensures needs are met for an individual without personal funds), and shall encourage each individual to select, purchase, and maintain own clothing and to dress as independently as possible.

When an individual has been assessed to need assistance with management of personal possessions, the operator shall record the individual's clothing and personal belongings within fourteen calendar days of admission and update the record at least annually. Any single item with a purchase price of fifty dollars or more shall be added to the record when acquired and deleted when discarded or lost.

An operator shall not discard an individual's clothing or personal belongings without the consent of the individual or guardian. If operation is transferred to another operator, the outgoing operator shall convey individuals' clothing and personal belongings to the incoming operator.

Current records for each individual maintained at the residential facility: (i) a photograph; (ii) legal status; (iii) individual service plan, including documentation of informed consent; (iv) signed authorization to seek medical treatment or documentation that attempts to secure it were unsuccessful; (v) medication and/or treatment records showing the prescriber and the date, time, and person who administered.

Records maintained in an accessible location and provided on request to the department: (i) former versions of (J)(1)(a) records; (ii) admission and referral records; (iii) all service documentation including notations of progress; (iv) medical and dental examination and immunization records; (v) records of major unusual incidents and unusual incidents; (vi) major unusual incident investigation files; (vii) reconciliations of the individual's account transaction record (rule 5123-2-07); (viii) records of negotiable items owned by the individual; (ix) records of clothing and personal belongings; (x) a written accounting within thirty calendar days following termination of residency covering circumstances of termination, new address, conveyance of records/ID/prescriptions/medications, disposition of clothing and belongings, and release or disposition of personal funds.
If operation of a residential facility is transferred from one operator to another, the outgoing operator shall convey the records specified in paragraph (J)(1) to the incoming operator.

All information contained in an individual's records shall be considered confidential. Records will be maintained in accordance with state and federal regulations and in such a manner to ensure their confidentiality and protect them from unauthorized disclosure.
An operator shall develop a records retention schedule for all records in accordance with applicable state and federal requirements.

Transfer and termination of services policies: an operator will allow each resident to remain in the residential facility and shall not initiate a transfer or termination of services unless: (a) necessary for the resident's welfare and needs can no longer be met without undue hardship on the operation; (b) the resident no longer needs or wants the services or chooses to move; (c) the resident is creating a significant risk of substantial harm to self, other residents, or staff; (d) nonpayment for the stay, including nonpayment of medicaid or other third-party payer; (e) the facility permanently reduces its capacity; or (f) the facility ceases to operate.

An operator shall not unlawfully discriminate because of disability, race, color, religion, national origin or ancestry, sex, or age, including failing to make reasonable accommodation to a person's physical, mental, or behavioral support needs to the extent required by law unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship.

Before initiating a transfer or termination of services, an operator shall: (a) notify the individual and the county board in writing via certified mail, with notice containing (i) the reason, (ii) the effective date, (iii) a summary of action taken by the operator, including working with the county board, to try to meet the resident's needs, (iv) the individual's right to appeal and the process, and (v) the telephone number and address of disability rights Ohio; (b) explain the transfer or termination and appeal rights in a manner the individual understands; and (c) record the reasons in the resident's record.

Notice must be made at least thirty calendar days before the transfer or termination, except when an emergency exists (the individual may return if the emergency conditions no longer exist before the thirty days expire). If the individual requests a hearing, the facility must maintain services or the availability of services until a decision is rendered unless an emergency exists. If the individual waives appeal rights in writing, the operator is not required to maintain services.

Administrative review process: the individual first appeals in writing to the governing board or administrator within seven calendar days of receipt of the notice; the governing board or administrator notifies the individual in writing of the outcome within five calendar days (by certified mail, with director contact information and explanation if denied); the individual then has five calendar days from receipt to appeal in writing to the director.

Mediation process: the individual and the operator shall attend a mediation meeting before the hearing process (legal representation not permitted); the department provides the mediator; the meeting is held within fifteen calendar days of receipt of the appeal; mediation is nonbinding unless all parties agree in writing; statements made in mediation cannot be used as evidence in later hearings or court proceedings.

Hearing process: the department grants a hearing to an individual who received a notice, attended mediation, and requests a hearing; the hearing officer (not the mediator) is appointed by the department; the hearing is held within thirty calendar days of the end of mediation; the burden of proof is on the operator; the hearing officer issues a written recommendation within ten calendar days; the director issues a written decision within five calendar days and may impose conditions.
If an operator fails to follow the requirements of this rule or fails to follow the decision of the director, the operator may be subject to adverse actions in accordance with rule 5123-3-06.

official.notes: No single DODD policy-review checklist or form (like Maryland's DD.APP.1.1 or California's LIC 281) was found for Ohio residential facility licensure. The items above come from the regulation sections that list required written policies and plans, as the instructions allow. Only 5123-3-01(C)(5)(b), (D)(7) and (E)(5) of 5123-3-04, (F)(6) of 5123-3-04, (F)(1) of 5123-3-02 and (C) of 5123-3-05 use explicit 'written policies/procedures/plan' wording. The other items are practice requirements that a facility's manual should address. Ohio has no prescribed manual order, so the sections above follow the rules' own paragraph order. Under ORC 5123.19, the applicant applies to the DODD Director. The Director conducts a pre-license survey, and DODD then reviews compliance (OAC 5123-3-06). That rule says a compliance review includes an examination of the facility's policies, and an abbreviated review focuses on background checks, behavioral support, medication administration, major unusual incidents and service delivery. The 5123-3-01 appendices A-D (training topics for administrators, DSPs, support staff and volunteers) set the content of the required training plan (D)(7)(a). They are linked from the rule page and were not read here. Fire safety and emergency plan: the rule requires approval by the state/local authority (fire marshal/local fire department, or Red Cross/county EMA) and sharing the plan with the county board. Related rules that apply but were not reviewed in this pass: 5123-2-02 (background checks), 5123-2-06 (behavioral support/restrictive measures), 5123-2-07 (individual funds), 5123-17-02 (incident reporting) and 5123-6 (medication). Person-centered planning (5123-3-03, effective 8/27/2026) puts assessment and the ISP with the county board's SSA for non-ICF/IID facilities. Its detailed ISP steps apply to ICF/IIDs and are omitted. For HCBS/IO waiver services (Homemaker/Personal Care under 5123-9-30; Shared Living under 5123-9-33), 5123-3-01(C)(3) requires a separate HCBS approval application, an ODM Medicaid provider agreement, and compliance with Chapter 5123-9. Those rules' service-specific requirements were not reviewed here. Verify them separately on codes.ohio.gov. The 5123-3-04 text was read from Cornell LII, so confirm it against the codes.ohio.gov version before submitting.
